brother’s room, fighting a legal battle he had little chance of winning.
How could he keep going? “I listen to Winston Churchill’s speeches,” he
said. “I drink too much. And I don’t want these people to get away with
this.” Some nights he dreamed about the case. His unconscious mind
churned over the words he’d written, trying to rephrase his story in a
way that would persuade a judge to see simple justice and return his
home to him.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span><img src="OEBPS/Images/sp.jpg" class="epubimage" alt="image" /><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>

By 2007, Gary Ozenne had some company among the litigants asking judges
to solve their problems. Roland Arnall had gone to court. This time he
was not a defendant but a plaintiff. In a case filed in federal court in
Tulsa, Oklahoma, Arnall claimed he’d been the victim of a
multibillion-dollar scam. His lawyers bandied terms that were similar to
ones that had been thrown at Arnall and his enterprises over decades of
litigation: Breach of contract. Misrepresentation. Fraud. Arnall claimed
he’d invested billions in oil and gas exploration and that he’d been
ill-treated by a business partner
w<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.3.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>ho was savvier than he was about the industry.

It all started, Roland and Dawn Arnall said, in early 2002, when they
met a man named Bippy Siegal. They were at a ski race in Sun Valley,
Idaho. Bippy had torn his ACL and was hobbling around the lodge on
crutches. Roland, Dawn said, felt sorry for him, and the couple went
over and struck up a conversation. As they talked, Bippy mentioned that
his father, Richard Siegal, was in oil and gas. He had a number of
wealthy investors, the son said, and his ventures made a lot of money
for them.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA293.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Roland had been a street peddler, a real-estate
developer, an S&L operator, and the owner of subprime mortgage
companies. Why not a Texas-style oilman? Richard Siegal told them, the
Arnalls claimed, that he had a track record of providing his investors a
\$3.50 to \$4 return on every dollar invested, and that the deal could
be structured to allow them to take a \$2 deduction for “intangible
drilling costs” for every dollar put into the venture. The Arnalls were
intrigued. With their subprime empire producing billions, the idea of
putting <span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page308"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>their money to work, and getting a huge tax
deduction in the bargain, was appealing.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Siegal came up with the name for the venture:
RoDa Drilling Company, for Roland and Dawn. It was all done on a
handshake. The key documents were left unsigned. “That was my husband,”
Dawn testified. “He did a lot of transactions on a handshake deal. He
had visceral reactions to people and trusted them and proceeded to have
business associations with them.” By early 2005, Dawn said, they had
plowed roughly \$1 billion into the enterprise. She became concerned
that they had yet to see much return on their investment. Even worse,
the IRS had initiated an audit of RoDa’s tax returns for
200<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>3 and 2004. The IRS, she said, was threatening
to disallow the Arnalls’ “intangible drilling cost” deduction,
suggesting they might have to pay as much as half a billion dollars in
taxes, penalties, and interest. That, she claimed, would mean that she
and her husband had lost no less than \$1.5 billion on their investment.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Roland and Dawn Arnall sued Richard Siegal in
July 2007. Siegal countersued, demanding that the Arnalls resume making
the payments on hundreds of millions of dollars in promissory notes
crucial to the structuring of the deal and the tax deductions. Siegal
said Roland Arnall had never been promised any particular return;
indeed, it was ludicrous to think anyone would guarantee results in a
venture as speculative as drilling for oil and gas. The deal fell apart,
Siegal said, only because Roland had quit paying his obligations.
Roland, in other words, had refused to pay on his loans
b<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>ecause he felt he had been a victim of fraud.
Many Ameriquest borrowers had sued to try to renounce their mortgages on
exactly those grounds.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span><img src="OEBPS/Images/sp.jpg" class="epubimage" alt="image" /><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA294.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>

Arnall resigned as ambassador to the Netherlands in early 2008. His
family said he needed to come home to help care for his grown son,
Daniel, who had been diagnosed with Hodgkin’s disease. He returned to
the United States and, on March 10, found himself in an Oklahoma
courtroom. He was scheduled to testify during pretrial proceedings in
the oil lawsuit. He never made it to the witness stand. He appeared
noticeably ill from the first day, and seemed to get worse as the
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page309"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>proceedings dragged on. At the end of the second
day, Arnall’s doctor advised him to return to Los Angeles and check into
the hospital. The next day he was diagnosed with esophageal cancer. It
had metastasized. Death was imminent. His lawyers asked the judge for
permission to schedule an immediate deposition, from his hospital bed if
necessary. The judge ordered that his testimony be taken on March 21.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

He died March 17, 2008. He was sixty-eight years old. The obituaries and
remembrances that followed noted his companies’ legal problems. They
also devoted space to the other side of his life story, recalling him as
a generous benefactor to animal shelters and as a founder, in the ’70s,
of the Simon Wiesenthal Center for Holocaust remembrance. “One of the
good guys died today,” Jon Daurio, a former Arnall aide, said. Governor
Schwarzenegger called Arnall “a wonderful and inspirational friend.”
Terry Rouch, who had worked for Arnall at Long Beach and Argent,
attended the memor<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>ial service. To Rouch it felt almost like a
political rally, with big-name officials dotting the crowd. He spotted
Los Angeles mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, Gray Davis, and Schwarzenegger.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Seventeen months later, the Arnalls’ lawsuit
against Richard Siegal came to an end. In August 2009, on the eve of
trial, the two sides cut a deal. The exact terms were secret. The
parties noted that, under their agreement, Siegal would have to obey the
judge’s order that he transfer title to the oil and gas properties in
question to the Roland and Dawn Arnall Trust. Roland Arnall, in death,
had won at least a partial victory.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The late subprime mogul’s legacy continued to be
a matter of dispute, however, in other courts. His younger brother,
Claude, filed court papers claiming that Roland and Dawn had stiffed him
out of a fortune. The claim involved Olympus Mortgage, a wholesale
mortgage lender the two brothers had founded in 2002. Each brother owned
half of the company, according to Claude. In 2004, Roland asked Claude
to sell him his half of Olympus. Roland, Claude said, offered him
roughly \$75 million to buy out his shares in the company. Over the next
fifteen months, he received close to \$30
mi<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA295.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>llion in payments from his brother. After that,
he said, Roland began putting him off, coming up with excuses for not
paying him the rest of what he
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page310"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>owed. After Roland’s death, Claude claimed, Dawn
repudiated the agreement, telling him: “You have nothing in writing.”

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Claude demanded \$47.6 million from Roland’s
estate. Dawn’s lawyers said there were no facts to support the idea that
there had been any “secret verbal agreement.” It was unreasonable, they
argued, to believe that Claude and Roland had entered into such a
business deal “without a single document being created.” It was an
argument that seemed at odds with Dawn’s testimony, in the oil case,
that Roland had often put together big deals based only on a handshake.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In federal court in Chicago, the multidistrict
litigation against Ameriquest and Argent neared its end. In early 2010,
borrowers began receiving letters notifying them that the two sides had
reached a tentative settlement. ACC Capital had agreed to dispose of
twenty-nine class-action cases by coughing up \$21 million to be
distributed among the plaintiffs’ attorneys and several hundred thousand
customers. The average payout to borrowers was expected to be perhaps
\$100 each. Because Ameriquest and its sister companies had quickly
offloaded its loans to Wall Street investors, and the
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>profits were transferred into Roland Arnall’s
personal accounts, ACC Capital had few assets left over by the time the
lenders closed shop. “Unfortunately, there isn’t much left for
borrowers,” Ben Diehl, an assistant attorney general in California who
had worked on the states’ investigation of Ameriquest, told the
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>As with the states’ \$325 million settlement,
the agreement to resolve the private class actions didn’t include any
admission of wrongdoing. Roland Arnall’s family members and business
associates were consistent in maintaining that his lenders hadn’t
engaged in systematic fraud. During the oil lawsuit, Siegal’s lawyers,
unable to question Roland, pressed Dawn with questions about her service
on the board of ACC Capital. They wanted to show that her husband’s
record for fair dealing and honest business practices was far from
unblemished.

<div class="extract">

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Q. Did you learn about certain sales practices
in your company?

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA296.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>A. My understanding…is that the settlement
included no admittance of guilt.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page311" class="calibre2"></span>

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Q. But nonetheless, you voted to pay \$325
million?

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

A. We had to.

Q. You say we had to. Why?

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>A. Because the attorney generals, if we hadn’t
paid it, would have suspended our licenses, and we couldn’t have
continued to operate in those states.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Q. As you sit here now, do you believe there was
any conduct within Ameriquest which would have been what we call
improper or unlawful sales practices?

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>A. There were some employees—as a matter of
fact, we brought in the FBI ourselves to prosecute those employees.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Q. Were there ever any findings or
determinations by the board made where you were present that it was the
general business practices of Ameriquest which was being attacked as
opposed to just particular rogue employees?

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>A. We agreed that it was not general business
practice. It was rogue employees.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Q. How many rogue employees?

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>A. I can’t answer that. I’m sorry.

</div>

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span><img src="OEBPS/Images/sp.jpg" class="epubimage" alt="image" /><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.10.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>

In 2009, ACORN founder Wade Rathke published a book on community
activism, <span class="italic">Citizen Wealth: Winning the Campaign to
Save Working Families</span>. He devoted a passage to his organization’s
settlement nearly a decade before with Ameriquest. Rathke said the July
2000 agreement had ensured “fairer, more transparent lending operations”
at the lender. While other companies, such as Household, had fought
ACORN’s efforts to clean up subprime, Rathke wrote, “Ameriquest
benefited by being an early responder in this campaign, quickly
realizing that it was smarter—and much cheaper—to settle and deal
wi<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA297.w.1.10.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>th the problems rather than endure a protracted
war in public, in the courts, and in the marketplace.” Rathke seemed
unaware of the record of fraud and exploitation that had continued at
Ameriquest. The company hadn’t dealt with its problems as a result of
its deal with ACORN. It hadn’t become fairer and more transparent. The
settlement with ACORN had helped the company wriggle free from an
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page312"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>FTC investigation and move forward with a seal
of approval from one of the nation’s biggest activist organizations.
Ameriquest had used the deal as cover that allowed it to grow bigger and
more predatory.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>While some were laboring to rewrite the history
of subprime’s rise and fall, others were trying to put its lessons to
work, or at least trying to put the ordeal behind them. For many, moving
on wasn’t easy.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Mark Glover, the former Ameriquest loan officer
in Los Angeles, continued to pursue his legal claim against Citigroup
and Smith Barney. He started a business that allowed struggling
homeowners to make money by renting out their homes as movie and TV film
locations. He drafted a memoir of addiction and struggle. He began
running marathons and became an advocate of long-distance running as a
way to fight addiction.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Travis Paules, who rose from branch manager to
vice president in his seven years at Ameriquest, wrote an
autobiographical novel. Its main character is named “Trevor Palmer.” He
gave the book a working title of <span class="italic">Ameriquest: The
Crack in the Liberty Bell</span>, then changed it to
<span class="italic">Whiteout</span>, an allusion to the company’s
tradition of altering and fabricating borrowers’ paperwork. After a
decade of carousing and “wickedness,” he said, he experienced a
transformation. Not long after he left Ameriquest, he was sitting in a
hotel room in Virginia. It was around midnight. He felt a presence in
the room<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>. Almost an electrical force. “God came down and
conked me on the head,” Paules recalled. “I had a vision of Jesus
standing behind me for some reason.” He went online and looked up the
Ten Commandments. “I found I’d broken them all,” he joked. He had broken
some of them, anyway. After being lost for so many years, he said, he
had found a new path. His second manuscript,
<span class="italic">180</span>, is a memoir of that journey.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA298.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Carolyn Warren, who worked as a loan officer for
Long Beach Mortgage and Ameriquest in the ’90s, became so fed up with
the slippery tactics that pervaded her industry that she, too, wrote a
book, <span class="italic">Mortgage Rip-Offs and Money Savers</span>.
She wanted to reveal some of the industry’s secrets and arm consumers
with information. The response from readers was so strong that she
decided to start a consulting business. Now, mortgage shoppers can
solicit her advice at
<span class="xrefURL"><a href="http://www.askcarolynwarren.com"
class="calibre6">www.askcarolynwarren.com</a></span>. She reviews loan
disclosures from <span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page313"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>various lenders, flagging junk fees that
applicants should demand that their lenders delete. She’s determined to
root out fees that sound important (and even seem to hint at romantic
bliss) but are in fact meaningless, such as “commitment fees” and
“satisfaction fees.” In 2009, she published a second book,
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Homebuyers Beware: Who’s
Ripping You Off Now?</span>

Bob Ney, the Ohio Republican who had been the mortgage industry’s go-to
guy in Congress, resigned from the House of Representatives and was
sentenced to thirty months in prison in the Jack Abramoff
influence-peddling scandal. Another player in the subprime saga who
spent time behind bars was Dickie Scruggs, the Mississippi plaintiffs’
attorney who had jetted out to Orange County to take on FAMCO and
Lehman. Four years after the big trial at the Reagan Courthouse, federal
authorities charged him with trying to bribe a judge in
Mi<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>ssissippi to influence how legal fees would be
split in an insurance case. Scruggs was sentenced to seven years in
prison.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Sheila Canavan, the lawyer who steered the
attack on FAMCO and Lehman, continued working to defend homeowners. She
helped win a settlement in a case against Bank of America’s former
subprime unit. She also continued working on the Lehman Brothers case as
it moved through the appeals process. The U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of
Appeals upheld the jury’s conclusion that Lehman had aided FAMCO’s
fraud. “Lehman admits that it knowingly provided ‘significant
assistance’ to First Alliance’s <span class="italic">business</span>,
but distinguishes that from providing substantial assistance to
<span class="italic">fraud</span>,” the judges wrote. “In a
sit<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>uation where a company’s whole business is built
like a house of cards on a fraudulent enterprise, this is a distinction
without a difference.” The appeals panel ordered the trial judge,
however, to recalculate the \$5.1 million award. The two sides agreed to
avoid a return to court. They were putting the final touches on a \$3.5
million settlement when Lehman filed for bankruptcy in September 2008.
The beneficiaries of the settlement took their place in line among
Lehman’s other creditors.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA299.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Prentiss Cox, the assistant attorney general in
Minnesota who led the states’ investigation of Ameriquest, took a job
teaching law at the University of Minnesota. He drafted the Minnesota
Subprime Borrower Relief Act, which would have allowed struggling
borrowers to <span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page314"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>delay foreclosure sales for a year. Republican
governor Tim Pawlenty vetoed the bill. Cox testified before Congress in
favor of a new federal Consumer Financial Protection Agency, telling a
House committee that predatory lending had been a disaster before it was
a crisis—it had harmed millions of Americans long before it was
recognized as the primary cause of the nation’s financial meltdown.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Chuck Cross, the banking regulator who believed
in hitting mortgage wrongdoers between the eyes, left Washington State
for Washington, D.C. He took a job at the Conference of State Bank
Supervisors, an association of state financial regulators. As he gave
speeches around the country, he warned regulators to keep an eye out for
dominant personalities—figures like FAMCO’s Brian Chisick, Countrywide’s
Angelo Mozilo, or Ameriquest’s Roland Arnall. When someone builds an
empire from scratch, Cross thought, they begin to feel accountable to no
one. They think they can get away with anything.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Brian Chisick looked back in anger, at Chuck
Cross and at others who had brought FAMCO down. Cross, he said, was “a
real villain”—a bureaucrat who joined a gang of class-action attorneys
on a witch hunt against his company. Somehow, in their minds, he said,
combining salesmanship and mortgages was deceptive and predatory. “The
legal system, in a word, sucks,” Chisick said. “We’ve got a terrible
system going here. I wish I could phrase that in a nicer way.” He was in
his seventies, and he’d been out of the mortgage business for almost a
decade. He had watched from the sidelines as Ameriquest
and<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> other lenders spun out of control and destroyed
the subprime market. “Wall Street made so much money available and
everyone was making so much money,” he said, “they just threw all of
underwriting criteria out the window and went for the numbers.”

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA300.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Roy Barnes, the Georgia governor who fought to
hold Wall Street accountable for abusive lending, spent six months doing
free legal work after he was voted out of office in 2003. He volunteered
with Atlanta Legal Aid’s Home Defense Program, working with Bill
Brennan, the dean of homeownership protection attorneys in America.
Barnes represented several Ameriquest borrowers, helping them save their
homes. By the start of 2010, Barnes was preparing to try to recapture
the governorship. Surveying the federal government’s
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page315"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>response to the financial crisis, he saw little
real reform. “We’re rebuilding the same system rather than trying to
make changes,” he said. The way he saw it, the only way to end the
scourge of “dirty paper” in the mortgage market was to have tough
“assignee liability” rules that forced everyone in the process to act
responsibly. Bankers, he said, should be required to ask themselves: “Do
I really want to make this loan? Because I may have to eat it.”

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

Carolyn Pittman, the Ameriquest borrower in Atlantic Beach, Florida,
continued to fight to hang on to her home. She prayed every day. “I’d
like to keep it if I can,” she told a newspaper reporter in 2007. “I
thought I would live here the rest of my life. What little life I have
left.” Fearing the worst, she had many of her things in boxes, stacked
in her dining room. Even as the company’s Wall Street confederate,
Deutsche Bank, pursued a foreclosure action against her, Ameriquest’s
sales machine continued to crank out mailings offering her yet another
loan. The letters came twice a
month<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>. Boldface type proclaimed: Slash Your Monthly
Payments.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Like Pittman, many of the borrowers in the loan
pool that held her mortgage were struggling to stay afloat. Of the
roughly three thousand loans that remained in her pool in the summer of
2009, 28 percent of the borrowers were delinquent, in bankruptcy, facing
foreclosure, or had already had their homes repossessed.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Greg Walling did his best to put his time as a
loan officer for FAMCO behind him. He once again worked in auto sales,
as a used-car manager at a dealership in Minnesota’s Twin Cities. He was
glad, he said, to have a job that didn’t require him to lie and
manipulate the way he’d been taught at FAMCO. He had a fantasy, though,
of winning the lottery and retiring, then devoting his time to giving
lectures to schoolchildren on how to be smart consumers and protect
themselves from rip-offs. He knew a thing or two about the subject.

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA301.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>He kept two boxes of documents from the FAMCO
case stacked on a shelf in a downstairs closet in his home. One winter
day—he thinks it was in 2005—he pulled the boxes off the shelf. It had
been seven years since he had left FAMCO, and two years since he’d
returned to Orange County and testified in the case against Lehman
Brothers. He opened the boxes and read through the affidavits, the
<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_page316"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA302"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA302.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA302.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>transcripts, and other documents. He thought:
“I’m done. I never have to look at these things again.” He felt lucky
that he’d been shamed into doing the right thing. He’d been given a
chance to play a part in exposing “The Monster” and all the other
devices and deceptions that had fueled the rise of FAMCO and the rest of
the subprime mortgage machine. He carried the boxes into the backyard to
his fire pit. Snow and ice crunched under his boots. He started a fire
and, one by one, dropped the documents into the flames. He made sure
everything was burned to ash.

</div>

</div>

<div class="calibre1">

<span id="9780805090468_bm01.html_GBS.PA302.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>

</div>

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html"></span>

<div class="calibre1">

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

</div>

<div id="9780805090468_not01.html_not01" class="frontMatterPage">

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page317" class="calibre2"></span>

<div class="calibre3">

## <span class="bold">Notes</span>

</div>

<div class="calibre3">

<span class="bold1">Introduction</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Mark Glover looked up from his cubicle</span>:
This account is based on a series of interviews with Mark Glover, as
well as an interview with a confidential source, a former coworker, who
confirmed many of the details provided by Glover. Some details came from
Glover’s lawsuit against the company, <span class="italic">Glover v.
Ameriquest</span>, Orange County Superior Court, 2004, as well as Los
Angeles Superior Court records, which document Glover’s check-fraud
case. (After Glover successfully completed probation, the case was
dismissed and his record was expunged.) Also helpful was
<span class="italic">Tamar Williams v.
Ameriquest</span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>, Orange County Superior Court, 2004. Williams,
a coworker of Glover, alleged in her lawsuit that Ameriquest “forged
income and asset documents, altered title reports, filed falsified grant
deeds, fabricated and falsified credit histories, and sold
non-beneficial loans.” Williams, who worked as a loan processor, claimed
loan files were taken away from her because she refused to falsify
documents, and that a supervisor directed her to shred falsified
paperwork to keep “dirty” loans from being turned up in an audit. When
she complained, Williams said, the company fired her rather than
investigate her <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.2.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>allegations. More generally, Williams’s and
Glover’s accounts of misbehavior at the company are remarkably similar
to accounts provided in my interviews with dozens of former Ameriquest
workers spread across the nation.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Close to midnight Pacific time</span>: Interview
with Wendell Raphael, a vice president who often made the calls.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He would just try to make you stretch”</span>:
Interview with Travis Paules.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA303.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Every closing”</span>: The loan officer, Omar
Khan, was quoted in a video produced by Angie Moreschi, a former TV
journalist, for the Consumer Warning Network, an online site created by
lawyers who represent borrowers suing Ameriquest and other subprime
lenders. Consumer Warning Network, <span class="italic">Ameriquest:
Anatomy of the Mortgage Meltdown</span>, Dec. 24, 2008.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page318" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>They buried the real documents</span>: This
fixed-rate decoy was described to me by Travis Paules in an interview.
See also Chris Arnold, “Former Ameriquest Workers Tell of Deception,”
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Morning Edition</span>,
National Public Radio, May 14, 2007, in which a former Ameriquest
employee from Florida, Tyson Russum, said: “Maybe the first couple of
documents they saw in their package were fixed rate, and then they would
slip in the adjustable rate docs at the end and then trash the
fixed-rate docs.”

<span class="italic">Carolyn Pittman</span>: Interviews with Carolyn
Pittman and her attorney, Lynn Drysdale of Jacksonville Area Legal Aid.
See also Caren Burmeister, “Beaches Woman Caught a Foreclosure Cycle,”
<span class="italic">Florida Times-Union</span>, Sept. 22, 2007; and
“Defendant’s Motion to Strike Count I, Answer,
Amende<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>d Affirmative Defenses, Amended Counterclaims
and Demand for Jury Trial,” <span class="italic">Deutsche Bank v.
Pittman</span>, Duval County (Fla.) Circuit Court, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Ameriquest Mortgage Securities, Inc. Mortgage
Pass-Through Certificates 2004-R7</span>: Details on this deal come from
documents filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission,
including the “Prospectus Supplement” dated June 30, 2004. UBS, J. P.
Morgan, and Citigroup served as “Joint Lead Managers” and “Joint Book
Runners,” meaning they structured the deal and took the lead in peddling
the resulting mortgage-backed securities to investors. Barclays Capital,
BNP Paribas, and Deutsche Bank served as “Co-Managers” they didn’t take
part in the “securitization” process but were
allocated<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> a portion of the securities to sell to their
clients. Details on investors in the deal came from Bloomberg and
<span class="italic">Mutual Fund Prospectus Express.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We are all here to make as much fucking
money”</span>: Quoted in testimony of Minnesota attorney general Lori
Swanson before the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, “Regarding
Predatory Mortgage Lending and Use of the Board’s Authority Under the
HomeOwnership and Equity Protection Act of 1994 (HOEPA) to Curb Abusive
Mortgage Lending,” July 14, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It was like college”</span>: Interview with
Travis Paules.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>At the branch where Mark Bomchill worked</span>:
Interview with Mark Bomchill, who worked as a loan officer at Ameriquest
from September 2002 to September 2003, as well as “Declaration of Mark
Bomchill” in <span class="italic">Ricci v. Ameriquest</span>, U.S.
District Court for Minnesota, 2005. In interviews, three others who
worked in Bomchill’s branch confirmed his version of how the office
operated. See also Mike Hudson and E. Scott Reckard, “Workers Say Lender
Ran ‘Boiler Rooms,’” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Feb.
4, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“People entrusting their entire home”</span>:
Interview with a confidential source. When I interviewed this former
loan officer in 2005, it was on the condition that his name not be used.
He said the time working at Ameriquest was so disturbing that he didn’t
want to be publicly associated with the company.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“The atmosphere was like this giant cocaine
party”</span>: Interview with Sylvia Vega-Sutfin.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“All roads lead to Lehman”</span>: Greg Griffin,
“Risky Mortgages,” <span class="italic">Denver Post</span>, Nov. 11,
2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the leading edge of a financial
hurricane”</span>: Bernard Connolly, “sub-prime Crisis Is the Edge of a
Financial Hurricane,” <span class="italic">Telegraph</span> (London),
Aug. 20, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA304.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Lehman never saw a subprime lender”</span>:
Interview with Sheila Canavan.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page319" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Roland could be the biggest bastard”</span>:
Interview with a confidential source, a
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>former Long Beach executive.

<span class="italic">“Roland was one of the most generous”</span>: A
former business partner of Arnall,
Jac<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>k Slomovic, quoted in “Roland Arnall,
Philanthropist and Ameriquest Founder,
D<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>ies at 68,” <span class="italic">Jewish
Journal</span>, Mar. 20, 2008.

<span class="italic">“a trail of bodies”</span>: Interview with Bob
Labrador, a banking
e<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>xecutive who worked for Arnall in the 1980s and
’90s.

<span class="italic">“I was screwed”</span>: Interview with Ray Mallel,
a longtime friend of Arnall and a
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>former top executive at Ameriquest.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“a good man”</span>: Interview with Mark
Schuerman, a former executive at Long Beach Savings.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Keep your enemies close”</span>: Interview with
Frank Curry, a former Long Beach Bank executive and Arnall confidant.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>1. Godfather</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The regulators pushed Arnall to
diversify</span>: Interview with Bob Labrador, former Long Beach Savings
executive.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He hated the regulators”</span>: Ibid.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“How soon can we get”</span>: This quote, as
well as Mark Schuerman’s account of his time working with Arnall, come
from a series of interviews with Schuerman, a former Long Beach Savings
executive.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall’s parents and early history</span>: Ron
Korver, “‘Sometimes You Have to Make a Fist’: U.S. Ambassador Roland
Arnall Thinks Europe Talks Too Much,” <span class="italic">De
Telegraaf</span>, April 21, 2007; “Roland Arnall, Envoy for Bush and the
U.S.,” <span class="italic">Het Parool</span>, April 21, 2007. See also
Arnall’s official biography on the Web site of U.S. Diplomatic Mission
to the Netherlands, “Ambassador Roland E. Arnall” Arnall’s speech to
Rotary Club members in Dordrecht, “The Future of the U.S. as a Nation of
Immigrants,” May 31, 2007; and Stephen Miller, “Subprime Pioneer Turned
to Diplomacy, Philanthropy,” <span class="italic">Wall Street
Journal</span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.12.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>, Mar. 22, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.13.0"
class="calibre2"></span>One story had Roland becoming an altar
boy</span>: Miller, “Subprime Pioneer” and interview with Frank Curry,
former Long Beach Bank executive and Arnall confidant.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.14.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“The next day I had my first major
fight”</span>: “Roland Arnall, Envoy for Bush and the U.S.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.15.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“My father returned”</span>: Korver, “‘Sometimes
You Have to Make a Fist.’”

<span class="italic">peddling flowers on street corners</span>: Arnall’s
biography at the U.S. Diplomatic Mission to the Netherlands.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.16.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall used the profits</span>: These passages
draw heavily from E. Scott Reckard, “Ambassador Nominee’s Company Is
Scrutinized,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Aug. 7,
2005, the only true profile that has ever been written of Arnall, who
did his best to keep his name and image out of the media after his
missteps in the ’60s.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA305.w.1.17.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In the decades to come, Snyder</span>: Various
news articles, including Bill Boyarsky, “Councilman Art Snyder Quits in
Surprise Move,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Jan. 3,
1985; Rick Orlov, “Art Snyder’s Conviction Upheld,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Daily News</span>, Feb. 25, 2000; Maura
Dolan, “Justices’ Ruling May Send Snyder to Jail,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Feb. 25, 2000.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page320" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall-Snyder land deal</span>:
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>
articles, including “Lincoln Heights Land Sale Gets Tentative OK,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Nov. 5, 1968; “Developer
Explains Delinquency in Land Bid Payment,” Mar. 13, 1969; “Snyder Asks
Refund to Developer in Land Deal,” Sept. 16, 1969; and “Council Upholds
Controversial Land Sale,” Oct. 2, 1969.

<span class="italic">“Real-estate development is a function”</span>:
Martin Mayer, <span class="italic">Nightmare on Wall Street: Salomon
Brothers and the Corruption of the Marketplace</span> (New York: Simon &
Schuster, 1993), p. 163.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“If there’s money available”</span>: Interview
with a confidential source, a
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>former Long Beach Savings executive.

<span class="italic">For a time, Arnall teamed with Beverly Hills
Bancorp</span>: Ibid.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In 1974, the bank filed for bankruptcy</span>:
“Bancorp on Coast Accused by S.E.C.,” <span class="italic">New York
Times</span>, Aug. 14, 1974; and <span class="italic">In the Matter of
Beverly Hills Bancorp</span>, 649 F.2d 1329 (9th Circuit, 1981).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>One friend who provided last-ditch loans</span>:
Interview with Ray Mallel, former Long Beach and Ameriquest executive.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>If S&Ls didn’t have to pay high rates</span>:
Much of the discussion of the S&L crisis is drawn from Stephen Pizzo,
Mary Fricker, and Paul Muolo, <span class="italic">Inside Job: The
Looting of America’s Savings and Loans</span> (New York: McGraw-Hill,
1989); and Kathleen Day, <span class="italic">S&L Hell: The People and
the Politics Behind the \$1 Trillion Savings and Loan Scandal</span>
(New York: W. W. Norton, 1993).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“we hit the jackpot”</span>: Ronald Reagan,
“Remarks on Signing the Garn–St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of
1982,” Oct. 15, 1982.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The new breed of S&L proprietors</span>: Pizzo,
Fricker, and Muolo, <span class="italic">Inside Job</span>, p. 13.

<span class="italic">A car-wash operator shocked</span>: Interview with
Bob Labrador.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>masquerading as an S&L</span>: This turn of
phrase comes from Bob Labrador.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall and his staff agonized</span>: Interview
with Bob Labrador, as well as with a confidential source.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It wasn’t done in a very overt way”</span>:
Interviews with Tom Tarter and Bob Labrador. Real-estate developer Bob
Champion, who partnered with Arnall on strip-mall projects in the late
1980s, says he never experienced problems with Arnall.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“intentional fraud”</span>:
<span class="italic">Romano v. Victory Square Ltd.</span>, filed Aug.
24, 1984, Los Angeles Superior Court.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.13.0"
class="calibre2"></span>the case was settled on confidential
terms</span>: In an e-mail correspondence, Kenneth Bley, the plaintiffs’
attorney, said a check of his firm’s files indicated the case had been
dismissed after the parties settled. He said he couldn’t disclose the
terms.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.14.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Don’t sit on your equity”</span>: These
examples are taken from Louise Story, “Home Equity Frenzy Was a Bank Ad
Come True,” <span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Aug. 15, 2008,
which includes an excellent compilation of advertisements urging
homeowners to borrow against their houses. See <span class="xrefURL"><a
href="http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2008/07/20/business/20debt-trap.html#"
class="calibre6">http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2008/07/20/business/20debt-trap.html#</a></span>.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.15.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Calling it a ‘second mortgage’”</span>:
Pei-Yuan Cha, a former vice president of Citicorp who ran the bank’s
consumer business in the 1980s, was quoted in Story, “Home Equity
Frenzy.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA306.w.1.16.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Hard-money and consumer-finance companies in the
1980s</span>: Some observers lump
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page321"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>consumer-finance companies into the term
“hard-money lending.” I prefer to make a distinction, defining
hard-money lenders as those that focused purely on mortgages and charged
the highest rates, often in the 20/20 range. Consumer-finance
operations’ rates were a bit lower, and their business models were
different enough, that it’s useful to distinguish between these strains
of lending. Interviews with Kathleen Keest, a staff attorney at the
Center for Responsible Lending and a former assistant attorney general
in Iowa, and with Mark Schuerman. See also Robert J. Hobbs,
Kathlee<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>n Keest, and Ian DeWall, “Consumer Problems with
Home Equity Loans, Second Mortgages, and Home Equity Lines of Credit,”
National Consumer Law Center, July 1989; Kathleen Keest, “Second
Mortgage Lending: Abuses and Regulation,” National Consumer Law Center,
Dec. 1991.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Miss Cash says ‘Yes’”</span>: The definitive
work on Landbank is Greg Raver-Lampman, “The Great White Loan Shark,”
<span class="italic">Regardie’s Magazine</span>, Apr. 1991. See also
coverage in the <span class="italic">Washington Post</span> and
<span class="italic">Virginian-Pilot</span>, as well as Mike Hudson,
“Little Relief for Consumers,” <span class="italic">Roanoke
Times</span>, Dec. 12, 1994.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Borrowers at finance companies”</span>: Quoted
in Walt Bogdavich, “After Deregulation: Critics Charge Lenders Exploit
Most Vulnerable,” <span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, Apr.
8, 1985.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>class-action settlements and Lennie Williams’s
case</span>: Larry Lopez, “Widow Battles Lending Giant for Home,”
Associated Press, Mar. 19, 1990; and Larry Lopez, “Transamerica Gives Up
Fight for Widow’s Home,” Associated Press, Mar. 22, 1990. Transamerica
said it had done nothing wrong. After a spate of bad publicity, it
settled the case, allowing Williams to stay in her home.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“To me, it’s fun and challenging”</span>: Carla
Lazzareschi, “Getting Ahead: Exploring Paths to Promotion,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Sept. 17, 1989.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Mortgage-backed securities had first
emerged</span>: Michael Lewis, <span class="italic">Liar’s Poker</span>
(New York: W. W. Norton & Company, 1989); Kurt Eggert, “The Great
Collapse: How Securitization Caused the Subprime Meltdown,”
<span class="italic">Connecticut Law Review,</span> vol. 41, no. 4,
2009; and the testimony of Christopher L. Peterson in “Subprime Mortgage
Market Turmoil: Examining the Role of Securitization,” a hearing before
the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs,
Subcommittee on Securities, Insurance, and Investment, Apr. 17, 2007.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>2. Golden State</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Guardian Savings and the Jedinaks</span>:
Interviews with Jude Lopez, a former Guardian executive, and with James
Gartland, a mortgage broker who worked with the Jedinaks over the years.
This discussion also draws upon extensive coverage in the
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span> and
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>. Paul Muolo and Mathew
Padilla, <span class="italic">Chain of Blame: How Wall Street Caused the
Mortgage and Credit Crisis</span> (Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons,
2008), pp. 61–63, includes much useful background on the Jedinaks,
including the “frat boy” quote.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“You’re going to end up with forty REO”</span>:
Interview with Jude Lopez.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“if the owner has a pulse”</span>: Elliot Blair
Smith and Jonathan Lansner, “Fortune
Turns<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA307.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span> for Guardian Savings,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Jan. 13, 1991.

<span class="italic">“cowboy capitalists”</span>: See Lisa McGirr,
<span class="italic">Suburban Warriors: The Origins of the New
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page322"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>American Right</span> (Princeton, N.J.:
Princeton University Press, 2001), pp. 28–30, 37–38, and 52.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">history of North America Savings</span>: Stephen
Pizzo, Mary Fricker, and Paul Muolo, <span class="italic">Inside Job:
The Looting of America’s Savings and Loans</span> (New York:
McGraw-Hi<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>ll, 1989), pp. 22 and 335, as well as copious
accounts filed by the <span class="italic">Orange County
Register</span>, <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>,
Associated Press, and other outlets.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“full burn”</span>: Much of the description of
boiler-room culture draws upon the definitive work, Robert J. Stevenson,
<span class="italic">The Boiler Room and Other Telephone Sales
Scams</span> (Urbana: University of Illinois Press, 1998).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Orange County as a white-collar and S&L crime
capital</span>: This discussion is drawn from numerous articles in the
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>,
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, and other publications.
See, for example, Henry N. Pontell and Kitty Calavita, “Orange County:
Thrift Fraud Capital of the United States,” <span class="italic">Journal
of Orange County Studies</span> 5–6 (Fall 1990–Spring 1991); Andre
Mouchard, “Criminal Culture,” <span class="italic">Orange County
Register</span>, Mar. 29, 2002 (a Q&A with Henry Pontell); and Jane
Apple-gate, “Fraud Agents Seize Records in 5 Raids in Metals Cases,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Apr. 17, 1987. Especially
helpful was Ma<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>rc Beauchamp, “Côte De Fraud,”
<span class="italic">Forbes</span>, Nov. 2, 1987, which documents Orange
County’s rise as the boiler-room capital of the United States.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“at a pace of just under one”</span>: Jonathan
Lansner, “Shame: OC a White-Collar Crime Hotbed,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Dec. 30, 1990.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I’ve worked cases where the lender”</span>:
Beauchamp, “Côte De Fraud.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Con men hate snow”</span>: Hal Lancaster,
“Beware!—The Fraud Farm: In Newport Beach, Calif., Scam Artists Find a
Place in the Sun,” <span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, Oct.
20, 1989.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“a modern-day version of the California gold
rush”</span>: McGirr, <span class="italic">Suburban Warriors</span>, p.
28.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Many of these people got too much”</span>:
Beauchamp, “Côte De Fraud.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>front companies they controlled</span>: In
addition to passages in <span class="italic">Inside Job</span> and
coverage in the <span class="italic">Orange County Register</span> and
the <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, two articles are
especially rich in details about Christensen and McKinzie’s frauds and
their lifestyles: Kathleen Sharp, “The Dentist and the Junk Blonde,”
<span class="italic">San Francisco Chronicle,</span> June 30, 1991, and
Richard W. Stevenson, “Untangling a Savings Failure,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, June 30, 1988.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>During a congressional hearing</span>: Ricardo
Sandoval, “Attack Launched on Fraud in OC,” <span class="italic">Orange
County Register</span>, July 27, 1990; Larry Liebert, “Probe of S&L
Corruption Stepped Up,” <span class="italic">San Francisco
Chronicle</span>, Dec. 8, 1989.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In Orange County alone</span>: Details of the
S&L debacle in Orange County and beyond are drawn from
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, especially “S&Ls and
the ’80s: A Few Tales of Those Times,” <span class="italic">Orange
County Register,</span> Apr. 11, 1999; Jonathan Lansner and Ann Imse,
“‘This Is an Epidemic’: Criminal Probes Creep Forward,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Nov. 8, 1987;
Jonathan Lansner, “Report Blames Thrift Failures on Misconduct,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Oct. 20, 1988;
Jonathan Lansner, “Actions on Irvine-Based Institutions Precipitated
Troubles,” <span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Dec. 5,
1989. Also helpful were Martin Mayer,
<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.12.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>The Greatest-Ever Bank Robbery</span> (New York:
C. Scribn<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA308.w.1.13.0"
class="calibre2"></span>er’s Sons, 1990); Pizzo, Fricker, and Muolo,
<span class="italic">Inside Job</span>; and Kathleen Day,
<span class="italic">S&L Hell: The People and the Politics Behind the
\$1 Trillion Savings and Loan Scandal</span> (New York: W. W. Norton &
Co., 1993).

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page323" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Charles Keating and Lincoln Savings</span>:
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span> coverage, including
Elliot Blair Smith, “Keating Ran S&L with Iron Hand, Ex-VP Says,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Sept. 19, 1991. Also
invaluable were Pizzo, Fricker, and Muolo, <span class="italic">Inside
Job</span>; Day, <span class="italic">S&L Hell</span>; L. J. Davis,
“Will Charlie Keating Ride Again?” <span class="italic">Washington
Monthly</span>, Mar. 1997; Richard W. Stevenson, “Independent Auditor
Criticizes Lincoln Savings and Loan,” <span class="italic">New York
Times</span>, Aug. 4, 1989; Michael Binstein and Charles Bowden,
<span class="italic">Trust Me: Charles Keating and the Missing
Billions</span> (New York: Random House, 1993); L. William Seidman,
<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>Full Faith and Credit: The Great S&L Debacle and
Other Washington Sagas</span> (New York: Times Books, 1993).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“captive” S&Ls</span>: William K. Black,
<span class="italic">The Best Way to Rob a Bank Is to Own One: How
Corporate Executives Looted the S&L Industry</span> (Austin: University
of Texas Press, 2005), pp. 81, 255, 265, and 289–90, and George A.
Akerloff and Paul M. Romer, “Looting: The Economic Underworld of
Bankruptcy for Profit,” <span class="italic">Brookings Papers on
Economic Activity</span>, vol. 1993, no. 2, pp. 53–56. Akerloff and
Romer provide lengthy excerpts of the FDIC’s lawsuit against Milken,
which alleged that Milken and his co-conspirators “cultivated a group of
persons who controlled S&Ls” and were willing to “follow the bidding of
the <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>Milken Group.” Milken, the FDIC alleged, used
his “\[r\]eady, repeated, easy access” to the enormous pool of capital
provided by the S&Ls’ depositors as part of a scheme to create the
illusion of heavy demand for Drexel-sponsored junk bonds and thus
artificially inflate their values. Milken denied wrongdoing, attributing
the government’s allegations to “blame-it-all-on-Milken scapegoating.”
Milken, other former Drexel employees, and Drexel’s insurance company
later settled the FDIC lawsuit as part of a \$1.3 billion global
settlement that extinguished civil claims in the junk-bond scandal.
Milke<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.1.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>n paid \$900 million of the settlement.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“sucking the blood”</span>: Benjamin J. Stein,
<span class="italic">A License to Steal: The Untold Story of Michael
Milken and the Conspiracy to Bilk the Nation</span> (New York: Simon &
Schuster, 1992), pp. 97–109.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Auditors found the S&L”</span>: Stevenson,
“Independent Auditor Criticizes.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the weak, meek and ignorant are always good
targets”</span>: Many of the details of Lincoln’s high-pressure
salesmanship come from James Bates, “Bond-Sale Rallies: It Was
Showtime,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Nov. 3, 1990.
I am indebted to Associated Press reporter Scott McCartney’s fine
coverage, including “Lincoln Savings Memo: The Week, Meek and Ignorant
Are Good Targets,” Associated Press, Sept. 8, 1990; and “Elderly Victims
of S&L Debacle Struggle to Pay Bills, Survive,” Associated Press, Oct.
10, 1989. Other sources include “Former Lincoln Investor Commits
Suicide,” Associated Press,
No<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>v. 28, 1990; Michael Connelly, “Victim of S&L
Loss Kills Self,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Nov.
29, 1990; Jim Tranquada, “S&L Failure Took Emotional Toll,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Daily News</span>, Dec. 2, 1990;
Michael Lev, “California Accuses Lincoln of Misleading Bond Buyers,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Mar. 3, 1990. In the
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, an attorney for Keating
maintained: “The bond salesmen were scrupulous in advising people that
these were subordinated debentures and were not insured by the federal
government. There always may be a small group who honestly felt they
were misled, but as to the vast majority I think it’s a case of
convenien<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA309.w.1.4.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>tly selective memory.”

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page324" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“it is precisely the ‘greed’”</span>: Quoted in
Jonathan Weil, “Greenspan’s ’63 Essay Foretold Subprime Inaction,”
Bloomberg News, Dec. 19, 2007.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">As Keating’s hired gun</span>: Mayer,
<span class="italic">Greatest-Ever Bank Robbery</span>, pp. 140 and
324–26.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“When I first met the people from
Lincoln”</span>: Nathaniel C. Nash, “Greenspan’s Lincoln Savings
Regret,” <span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Nov. 20, 1989.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Greenspan had advised that S&Ls</span>: In
explaining his views on so-called direct investments in big commercial
deals for S&Ls, Greenspan told the <span class="italic">New York
Times</span> in 1989: “If you give me two institutions, one that has a
mix of short-term direct investments and long-term mortgages properly
capitalized, or the same financing structure but invested only in
long-term mortgages, I would say the first institution may well be
safer.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He may have seen himself in Milken”</span>:
Interview with Bob Labrador. Labrador told me he was grateful for
Arnall’s restraint in resisting the temptation to gamble Long Beach’s
future on Milken’s junk. “Thank goodness he never let me do it,”
Labrador said. Columbia Savings, like other thrifts within Milken’s
orbit, failed. The government seized Columbia in 1991 at a cost to
taxpayers of more than \$1 billion.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>3. Purge</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In the summer of 1990, Greenwich Capital</span>:
John Gittelsohn, “How Subprime Lending All Started in O.C.,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Dec. 30, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It was a significant transitional
moment”</span>: Interview with Bob Labrador.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>He eventually stopped driving</span>: Another
account said Arnall hired the chauffeur to drive and maintain his car
after he forgot to put oil in his Porsche and burned out the engine.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He was demanding”</span>: Interview with Frank
Curry, a former Long Beach executive.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He was an idol worshipper”</span>: Interview
with Ray Mallel.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Long Beach fudged its books</span>: Interview
with a confidential source.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“What we’re seeing is people”</span>:
Allegations of questionable practices at Guardian were reported in the
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span> and the
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>. See especially
Elliot Blair Smith, “S&L Loan Practices Criticized,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Feb. 13, 1991; and
Elliot Blair Smith, “S&Ls, Easy Lending Terms Hid Credit Exploitation,
Regulators Say,” <span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>,
Nov. 29, 1992. See also <span class="italic">In the Matter of Russell M.
Jedinak</span>, Before the Office of Thrift Supervision, Dec. 8, 1995,
Order No. SF-95-023, and <span class="italic">In the Matter of Rebecca
Manley Jedinak</span>, Before the Office of Thrift
Supervision,<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.12.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> Dec. 8, 1995, Order No. SF-95-024.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.13.0"
class="calibre2"></span>delinquency rates of 23 to 51 percent</span>:
Mary McGarity, “Hot Product or Hot Potato?”
<span class="italic">Mortgage Banking</span>, Oct. 1, 1994. In early
1994 Standard & Poor’s downgraded Guardian’s credit ratings on a series
of securities backed by six-month adjustable-rate mortgages made by the
S&L from 1988 to 1991. S&P said its experience with Guardian prompted it
to rethink its criteria on subprime mortgages. “We’re trying to put in
place some type of extra protection to prevent what happened with
Guardian from happening again,” an S&P executive said.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA310.w.1.14.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He’s a high-powered salesman”</span>: Quoted in
Elliot Blair Smith, “Regulators Seize Guardian,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, June 22, 1991.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page325" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“something that really wasn’t broken”</span>:
Interview with Jeanne Powers, a former Long Beach employee.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“control thing”</span>: Interview with Mark
Schuerman.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>He’d crossed out</span>: Paul Muolo and Mathew
Padilla, <span class="italic">Chain of Blame: How Wall Street Caused the
Mortgage and Credit Crisis</span> (Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons,
2008), p. 63. Details of Quality’s start-up phase come from
<span class="italic">Chain of Blame</span> as well as from interviews
with two executives who worked for the Jedinaks at Quality.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the first subprime/Wall Street joint
venture”</span>: Frank J. Fabozzi, ed., and Robert Paul Molay,
<span class="italic">Subprime Consumer Lending</span> (New Hope, Pa.:
Frank J. Fabozzi Associates, 1999), p. 166.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>lion on a leash and the million-dollar pile of
cash</span>: Interviews with Jude Lopez and James Gartland. Gartland
worked as an outside broker feeding loans to Quality and later became an
in-house branch manager for the company.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Anything aggressive”</span>: Interview with
Adam Levine, a loan officer at Long Beach in the early 1990s.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“signs of initiative and loyalty”</span>: Muolo
and Padilla, <span class="italic">Chain of Blame</span>, p. 64.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>\$2 million a year in lawyers’ fees</span>:
Interview with Jude Lopez. Lopez said that when the Jedinaks finally
sold Quality Mortgage in 1996, the company still had more than thirty
consumer lawsuits pending.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The lawsuits claimed Quality socked</span>: See,
for example, <span class="italic">Ward v. Quality</span>, U.S. District
Court for Northern District of California, 1995, which claimed Quality
and mortgage brokers that fed it customers “failed to make proper
disclosures under federal and state law…charged improper fees, made
loans which failed to provide benefits allegedly promised, and made
misrepresentations about the loans.” This class action was settled in
1998. Quality and the brokers denied wrongdoing.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“corrupted hundreds of small mortgage
brokers”</span>: <span class="italic">Willis v. Quality</span>, U.S.
District Court for the Middle District of Alabama, 1994.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“manipulation and deception”</span>: See Hawaii
Intermediate Court of Appeals’ July 31, 2002, ruling in
<span class="italic">Ocwen v. Russell</span>, on appeal from the Third
Circuit Court of Hawaii.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Fleet Finance</span>: I reported extensively on
the company’s practices in the early 1990s. See Michael Hudson, “Loan
Scams,” <span class="italic">APF Reporter</span>, a publication of the
Alicia Patterson Foundation, 15:2, 1992; and Michael Hudson, “Stealing
Home,” <span class="italic">Washington Monthly</span>, June 1992. Much
of my investigation built on the fine coverage of Fleet in the
<span class="italic">Boston Globe</span>, including Peter S. Canellos
and Gary Chafetz, “In 2 Regions, Fleet Under Fire for Buying
High-Interest Loans,” <span class="italic">Boston Globe</span>, May 22,
1991; and Peter S. Canellos, “Profitable Fleet Finance’s Ethics
Questioned,” <span class="italic">Boston Globe</span>, June 9, 1991. The
<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.11.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>Atlanta Journal-Constitution</span> also did
excellent reporting on Fleet, including Jill Vejnoska, “Loan Trap,”
<span class="italic">Atlanta Journal-Constitution</span>, Oct. 11, 1992,
which told Lillie Mae Starr’s story in rich detail.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA311.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It’s like finding a ten-dollar bill”</span>:
This passage draws on many interviews with Brennan and those who know
him as well as Tammy Joyner, “People in Business: Up Close/William J.
Brennan Jr.,” <span class="italic">Atlanta Constitution</span>, Jan. 22,
2008. A former colleague, Hugh O’Donnell, described Brennan’s continual
shock over injustice, in a letter dated May 10, 1993, nominating Brennan
for an award from the state bar of Georgia.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page326" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Brennan, Rothbloom, and Barnes used the
power</span>: Interviews with Howard Rothbloom, Roy Barnes, and Barnes’s
aide Chris Carpenter, as well as news articles in the
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Atlanta
Journal-Constitution</span>; Robert Berner and Brian Grow, “They Warned
Us About the Mortgage Crisis,” <span class="italic">BusinessWeek</span>,
Oct. 9, 2008; and CBS News, “A Matter of Interest” (transcript),
<span class="italic">60 Minutes</span>, Nov. 15, 1992.

<span class="italic">Curry had to fire</span>: Interview with Frank
Curry.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>One of the consumer-finance transplants</span>:
Interviews with Terry Rouch, a loan officer at Long Beach from 1992 to
1995.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“People taking shortcuts”</span>: Interview with
Wendell Raphael, a manager in the mortgage unit at Long Beach in the
1990s.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>late-night loan closings</span>: In a 1993
lawsuit, a couple claimed a Long Beach salesman tricked them into
signing an unfair mortgage by arranging the loan closing “at a dimly lit
restaurant, late at night.” See <span class="italic">Kellogg v. Long
Beach Bank</span>, Riverside County (Calif.) Superior Court, Sept. 13,
1993.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Even back in the mid-’90s</span>: Adam Levine,
who worked at Long Beach during the same period as Rouch, doesn’t recall
seeing anyone forging borrowers’ signatures. But he said it was common
for workers to use bogus data when they drew up “profit and loss”
statements analyzing borrowers’ monthly income and spending.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>They worried that Long Beach</span>: See October
9, 1992, “Supervisory Agreement” between Long Beach and the Office of
Thrift Supervision.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I’m done”</span>: Interview with Bob Labrador.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>When another aide left</span>: See Alyssa Katz,
<span class="italic">Our Lot: How Real Estate Came to Own Us</span> (New
York: Bloomsbury USA, 2009), pp. 54–63, as well as
<span class="italic">Long Beach Mortgage Co. v. Manuel Palazzo</span>,
Orange County Superior Court, 1996.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Russ and Becky admitted no wrongdoing</span>: I
tried to contact the Jedinaks through their former attorney as well as
through Jude Lopez, their former aide at Guardian and Quality. Neither
the attorney nor Lopez knew how to reach the couple. Lopez said he
hadn’t been in touch with Russ for several years; he’d heard that Russ
might be living in the Caribbean. To get the Jedinaks’ side of the
story, I relied on Russ Jedinak’s statements in news articles as well as
interviews with Lopez, who defended the couple’s business practices as
reasonab<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>le and aboveboard.

<span class="italic">a 44 percent ownership stake</span>: Edmund
Sanders, “BNC Mortgage Plans Stock Sale to Public,”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Oct. 25, 1997.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>4. Kill the Enemy</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“You can securitize virtually
everything”</span>: Suzanne Woolley with Stan Crock, “‘You Can
Securitize Virtually Everything,’”
<span class="italic">BusinessWeek</span>, July 20, 1992.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.13.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“When everybody wants to securitize”</span>:
Suzanne Woolley, “What’s Next, Securitized Bridge Tolls?”
<span class="italic">BusinessWeek</span>, Sept. 2, 1996.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.14.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“one of the best Southern patriots”</span>: This
history of Lehman Brothers from its founding through the 1980s is
indebted to Ken Auletta, <span class="italic">Greed and Glory on Wall
Street: The Fall of the House of Lehman</span> (New York: Random House,
1986).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA312.w.1.15.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“narrowly focused pipsqueak”</span>: Andy
Serwer, “Improbable Power Broker.” <span class="italic">Fortune</span>,
Apr. 17, 2006.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page327" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.0.0.0"
