class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The architect of Lehman’s comeback</span>: Steve
Fishman, “Burning Down His House,” <span class="italic">New York
Magazine</span>, Nov. 30, 2008, is a rich source of background on Dick
Fuld.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“bristling class resentment”</span>: Fishman,
“Burning Down His House.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“The major corporate names which Lehman Brothers
desires”</span>: Auletta, <span class="italic">Greed and Glory</span>,
p. 43.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He was extremely outgoing”</span>: Jeffrey
Cohan and Jonathan D. Silver, “A Coal Town’s Boom Turns to Bust,”
<span class="italic">Pittsburgh Post-Gazette</span>, Oct. 20, 1999.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Keystone knew nothing”</span>: This account
draws heavily on the work of Bill Archer of the
<span class="italic">Bluefield</span> (W.Va.) <span class="italic">Daily
Telegraph</span> and Lawrence Messina of the
<span class="italic">Charleston</span> (W.Va.)
<span class="italic">Gazette</span>, as well as coverage by the
Associated Press and the <span class="italic">American Banker</span>.
See also John R. Engen, “The Collapse of Keystone,”
<span class="italic">Bank Director Magazine</span>, 2nd quarter 2001;
Jeffrey Cohan and Jonathan D. Silver, “A Coal Town’s Boom Turns to Bust”
Terence O’Hara, “Big Bank Scandal Unearthed in Tiny W. Va. Town,”
<span class="italic">Washington Post</span>, Oct. 19, 1999; Thomas
Fields-Meyer and Susan Gray, “Dashed Hopes: A Devastating Bank Failure
Leav<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>es a Shocked Little Town to Pick Up the Pieces,”
<span class="italic">People</span>, 52 (21), Nov. 29, 1999; Timothy
Roche, “Poor Town, Rich Bank,” <span class="italic">Time</span>, Nov. 1,
1999. Useful government documents include Office of Inspector General,
U.S. Department of Treasury, “Material Loss Review of the First National
Bank of Keystone,” OIG-00-067, Mar. 10, 2000; filings in various
Keystone-related civil and criminal cases in the U.S. District Court for
the Southern District of West Virginia, including
<span class="italic">FDIC v. Mitchell et al.</span>,
<span class="italic">Coast Partners et al. v. FDIC</span>, and
<span class="italic">Grant Thornton LLP v. FDIC</span>; and the Fourth
Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals’ Oct. 25,
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.4.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>2007, ruling in <span class="italic">FDIC v.
Sean Bakkebo et al.</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I thought the place sucked”</span>: Eric
Hibbert’s reaction to FAMCO is based on his March 11, 2003, testimony in
<span class="italic">Austin et al. v. Chisick et al.</span>, U.S.
District Court for the Central District of California, 2001.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Brian Chisick was an immigrant</span>:
Interviews with Brian Chisick as well as his 2001 testimony in
<span class="italic">FTC v. First Alliance</span>, U.S. District Court
for the Central District of California, 2000.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“professional problem solver:”</span> Brian
Tracy, <span class="italic">The 100 Absolutely Unbreakable Laws of
Business Success</span> (San Francisco: Berrett-Koehler Publishers,
Inc., 2002), pp. 191 and 202.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In October 1987, Myrtle and Elmer Rogers</span>:
Chris Woodyard, “Couple to Get \$1 Million for Loan Damages,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Oct. 16, 1987.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We did nothing wrong”</span>: Interview with
Brian Chisick.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“In many cases, the victims do not even
know”</span>: The state’s investigation was covered in the
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span> and
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>. See especially Al
Delugach, “State Suit Alleges Mortgage Firm ‘Redlined’ Blacks,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Aug. 11, 1988; Al
Delugach, “Ruling Postponed on Orange Loan Broker Accused by State of
Racial Discrimination,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>,
Aug. 12, 1988; Dan Weikel, “OC Lender Charged with Discrimination in
Black Neighborhoods,” <span class="italic">Orange County
Register</span>, Aug. 11, 1988; United Press International,
“Discrimination Denied by Lender,” <span class="italic">The
Record</span>, Aug. 14, 1988; and
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA313.w.1.10.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>Jonathan Weber, “First Alliance Agrees to Pay
\$436,000 to Settle Bias Suit,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles
Times</span>, Oct. 6, 1989.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page328" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“stage a Pearl Harbor attack”</span>: United
Press International, “Discrimination Denied by Lender.”

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">Robert N. Kwong’s battle with FAMCO</span>:
Interview with Robert Kwong, a former staff attorney with the California
Department of Corporations.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It was really insulting”</span>: Interview with
Brian Chisick.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>John Dewey and FAMCO’s early
securitizations</span>: Interview with John Dewey, a former FAMCO
executive.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I wouldn’t give him the time of day”</span>:
Interview with Brian Chisick.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Dunning <span class="italic">case and Robert
Goldstein’s allegations</span>: Both <span class="italic">Dunning v.
First Alliance</span>, 1989, and <span class="italic">Goldstein v.
McPhillips et al.</span>, 1994, which contained Goldstein’s harassment
and assault claims, were filed in Alameda County (Calif.) Superior
Court.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It is a sweat shop”</span>: The quotations come
from Eric Hibbert’s undated four-page memo, “Review of First Alliance
Mortgage Company,” which was based on his July 25–26, 1995, visit to
FAMCO’s headquarters in Orange, California.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“very capable and well informed”</span>: Undated
memorandum from Lehman Brothers executives Martin Harding, Kurt Locher,
and Stan Labanowski to the firm’s Investment Banking Mortgage Securities
Commitment Committee.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Lehman Brothers would enthusiastically
welcome”</span>: Letter from Martin P. Harding, a Lehman Brothers
managing director, to Mark Mason, chief financial officer of First
Alliance Mortgage Co., Nov. 29, 1995.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Yeah, we had a beauty show”</span>: Testimony
of Brian Chisick in <span class="italic">FTC v. First Alliance</span>.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>5. The Big Spin</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Bill Clinton’s attorney general, Janet
Reno</span>: Interview with Alexander Ross, a lawyer in the U.S. Justice
Department’s Civil Rights Division during the Clinton administration.
“Janet Reno was wonderful in this regard,” Ross said. “There was no
doubt in anybody’s mind that she wanted these cases pushed.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>What, Arnall asked</span>: Ibid.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.13.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The Justice Department’s statistical
analysis</span>: Complaint and settlement agreement in
<span class="italic">USA v. Long Beach Mortgage Company</span>, U.S.
District Court for the Central District of California, 1996.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.14.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“When you’ve got an elderly black woman”</span>:
Interview with Alexander Ross.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.15.0"
class="calibre2"></span>salespeople’s expectations about their
customers</span>: See, for example, Ian Ayers, “Fair Driving: Gender and
Race Discrimination in Retail Car Negotiations,”
<span class="italic">Harvard Law Review</span> 104(817) (1991). This
study used paired testers who fit middle-class profiles and employed a
uniform bargaining strategy. The testers visited ninety car dealers in
the Chicago area and found salespeople’s final offers favored white male
customers by a large margin; the markups on sticker prices were 40
percent higher for white women, double for black men, and triple for
black women.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.16.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Betty Lacey</span>: Kathy Lynn Gray, “Woman Fell
Prey to Lending Ploy,” <span class="italic">Columbus Dispatch</span>,
June 24, 2000.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA314.w.1.17.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Long Beach had other allies</span>: Jaret
Seiberg, “Regulators Asked to Spell Out Liability in the Event of Bias
Violations by Mortgage Brokers,” <span class="italic">American
Banker</span>, July 11, 1996; Jaret Seiberg, “Settlement of Bias Case
Against Calif. Lender Criticized for Vagueness,”
<span class="italic">American Banker</span>, Sept. 16, 1996; “Justice
Delays Move on Lending Bias <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page329"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Case,” <span class="italic">Mortgage
Marketplace</span>, July 8, 1996; Tim W. Ferguson, “Lender Beware (Home
Loan Quotas),” <span class="italic">Forbes</span>, Dec. 2, 1996; and
Kenneth Harney, “Minorities, Women, Elderly Often Pay More,”
<span class="italic">Chicago Sun-Times</span>, Sept. 13, 1996.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“If you listened to Bill Clinton”</span>:
Ferguson, “Lender Beware (Home Loan Quotas).”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>the investigation was led by Deval
Patrick</span>: Patrick’s biography is based on Scott Helman, “Beating
Odds, a Uniter Rose from Chicago’s Tough Side,”
<span class="italic">Boston Globe</span>, May 24, 2006.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>an extensive lineup of buck passers</span>: See
Kurt Eggert, “Held Up in Due Course: Predatory Lending, Securitization,
and the Holder in Due Course Doctrine,” <span class="italic">Creighton
Law Review</span> 35(503) (2002).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Some industry insiders grumbled</span>: Heather
Timmons, “Calif. Bias Settlement Brings Sighs of Relief from Industry,”
<span class="italic">American Banker</span>, Sept. 11, 1996; Seiberg,
“Settlement of Bias Against Calif. Lender” and “Fair Lending Settlement
Does Not Affect Overages,” <span class="italic">National Mortgage
News</span>, Sept. 16, 1996.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The leaders of these groups said Arnall
impressed</span>: Those leaders were Ricardo Byrd of the National
Association of Neighborhoods, Shanna Smith of the National Fair Housing
Alliance, and Wade Henderson of the Leadership Conference on Civil
Rights.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall renewed his support</span>: Mike Hudson,
“Ameriquest’s Ties to Watchdog Groups Are Tested,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, May 22, 2005. In 2004,
for example, Ameriquest gave a total of some \$800,000 to seven watchdog
groups, including \$250,000 to the Leadership Conference on Civil
Rights.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We sat around my conference table”</span>:
Jonathan Peterson, “Ameriquest Exec Has Unexpected Backers,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Nov. 21, 2005. See also
Tory Newmyer, “Arnall Secures Outside Help,” <span class="italic">Roll
Call</span>, Dec. 5, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall would suggest that Long Beach had
won</span>: Paul Muolo and Mathew Padilla, <span class="italic">Chain of
Blame: How Wall Street Caused the Mortgage and Credit Crisis</span>
(Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons, 2008), pp. 73–74. According to Muolo
and Padilla, Countrywide Financial CEO Angelo R. Mozilo met with Arnall
sometime in the early 2000s, with Mozilo coming away from the meeting
believing Long Beach had come under the feds’ scrutiny because of a
single freelance mortgage broker. “He eventually won the case,” Mozilo
said.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>His timing was a bit off</span>: Barnaby Feder,
“A Risky Business Gets Even Riskier,” <span class="italic">New York
Times</span>, Feb. 12, 1997; and Heather Timmons’s coverage in
<span class="italic">American Banker</span>, including “Winners and
Losers from the Subprime Crunch,” Feb. 21, 1997, and “Calif. Lender
Plans IPO, But Timing Could Be Problem,” Apr. 17, 1997.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the walking dead”</span>: See Aaron Elstein, “9
Subprime Lenders for Sale, May Die,” <span class="italic">American
Banker</span>, May 1, 1997; Heather Timmons, “Once Burnt, Big Investors
Now Twice as Cautious About Finance Companies,”
<span class="italic">American Banker</span>, June 20, 1997, and Aaron
Elstein, “The Cocaine Addiction of Our Industry,”
<span class="italic">American Banker</span>, July 1, 1997.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA315.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Even if you get sick”</span>: Documents in
<span class="italic">In Re: Marriage of Arnall</span>, Los Angeles
Superior Court, filed in 1996 and reopened in 2005. Much of this passage
is drawn from Sally Arnall’s account of the divorce negotiations,
detailed in “Declaration of Miriam Sally Arnall,” June 15, 2005. Also
helpful was E. Scott Reckard’s reporting in the <span class="italic">Los
Angeles Times</span>, including “Ex-Wife of Loan Exec Asks for Probe,”
Aug. 22, 2005, and “Loan Exec Loses Ruling to Ex-Wife,” Aug. 25, 2005.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page330" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“in a shade of gold”:</span> For this and other
biographical details, see the profile of Angelo Mozilo in Gretchen
Morgenson and Geraldine Fabrikant, “Countrywide’s Chief Salesman and
Defender,” <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Nov.
11, 2007.

<span class="italic">Carolyn Warren:</span> Interview with Carolyn
Warren, a Long Beach/Ameriquest loan officer in the 1990s, as well her
book, <span class="italic">Mortgage Rip-Offs and Money Savers: An
Industry Insider Explains How to Save Thousands on Your Mortgage or
Re-finance</span> (Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons, 2007).

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>6. The Track</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Greg Walling:</span> Interviews with Greg
Walling, a former loan officer for First Alliance Mortgage, as well as
his testimony in court proceedings against FAMCO.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Patty Sullivan, FAMCO’s training
director:</span> Patty Sullivan’s background is drawn from her December
3, 5, and 6, 2001, testimony in <span class="italic">FTC v. First
Alliance</span>, U.S. District Court for the Central District of
California, 2000. Sullivan testified that at one point she owned 49
percent of an auto dealership in California.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Walling’s training and the “Track” sales
pitch:</span> Interviews with Greg Walling, as well as testimony by
Walling, Terence LaFrankie, and Matt Winston, and lawsuits filed by
state authorities in Minnesota, Illinois, and other jurisdictions.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“nothing misleading or deceptive”:</span>
Interview with Brian Chisick.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“don’t hide the ball”:</span> Patty Sullivan’s
2001 testimony in <span class="italic">FTC v. First Alliance</span>. The
whole point of FAMCO’s sales presentation was not to take advantage of
people, Sullivan testified, but rather to find out how to meet their
needs. “When you’re speaking to people as a salesperson…you’re always
looking for…opportunities to sell benefits. For instance, if you see
someone who had been working for thirty years was injured on the job and
was off for two years, you would expect to see…that perhaps he was
living on his credit cards until he could get back to work. So you would
begin to get<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.7.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> an idea of what benefits this person would be
looking for in a loan.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Chuck Cross:</span> Interviews with Chuck Cross,
the former director of the Division of Consumer services, Department of
Financial Institutions, Washington State.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>He had gone after a preacher:</span> See
<span class="italic">People v. Honeywood Development</span>, Cook County
Circuit Court.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Tom James and the Celeketics:</span> Interview
with Tom James, a lawyer for the state of Illinois. Background on the
Celeketics’ loan also came from Alex Rodriguez and Bill Rumbler, “Loan
Officers Told to Mislead, Ex-worker Says,” <span class="italic">Chicago
Sun-Times</span>, Apr. 4, 1999. “I went to therapy because of this,”
Gloria Celeketic told the <span class="italic">Sun-Time</span>s. “I’m
working very hard for my money. When this amount was stolen from me, you
can just imagine how I felt.”

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>7. Buried</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA316.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Gary Ozenne and Ameriquest Mortgage:</span>
Interviews with Gary Ozenne, as well as documents in the numerous legal
actions he filed in an effort to reclaim his home. They include
<span class="italic">Ozenne v. Chase Manhattan et al</span>., Riverside
County Superior Court, 2002. Among the most helpful documents was
“Declaration of Gary L. Ozenne in
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page331"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Support of Petition for a Writ of Mandamus,”
filed Feb. 20, 2009, with the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

<span class="italic">Paules picked up the phone:</span> Travis Paules’s
personal and professional history is drawn from interviews with Paules,
who was forthcoming about Ameriquest’s practices and his own behavior
during his time as a branch manager, area manager, regional manager, and
vice president at the company. He said he had experienced a religious
awakening after he left the company, which freed him to talk frankly
about those days. “I was a different person then,” he told me.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Securitizations are all about
guesswork”:</span> Gary Silverman and Debra Sparks, “Asset-Backed
Gambling? The Sector Is More Hazardous Than Many Investors Realize,”
<span class="italic">BusinessWeek</span>, Oct. 26, 1998.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Lehman Brothers’ stock price fell:</span> The
passage on the effects of the Long-Term Capital Management debacle and
currency crises on Lehman Brothers are based on Ianthe Jeanne Dugan,
“Battling Rumors on Wall St.; Lehman Brothers Chairman Launches
Aggressive Defense,” <span class="italic">Washington Post</span>, Oct.
10, 1998.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“They suck”:</span> Testimony by Eric Hibbert,
during the 2003 trial of <span class="italic">Michael Austin et al. v.
Brian Chisick et al</span>., part of the <span class="italic">In Re:
First Alliance Mortgage Company</span> litigation in U.S. District Court
in Santa Ana, California, which sorted out FAMCO’s bankruptcy and the
various allegations against FAMCO and Lehman Brothers.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“absolutely amazing at ferreting”:</span>
Remarks from an eight-page memo, dated February 1, 1999, that Hibbert
wrote during Lehman’s “due diligence” review of the lender.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The consensus among Lehman executives:</span>
The review team’s findings come from a confidential memo signed by a
dozen executives in preparation for a February 11, 1999, meeting of
Lehman’s Investment Banking Commitment Committee. Among those receiving
copies of the memo was Lehman chief executive Dick Fuld.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We are in the business of doing
transactions”:</span> Testimony of Steve Berkenfeld in
<span class="italic">Austin v. Chisick</span>.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Delta:</span> Coverage in
<span class="italic">Newsday</span> and other New York–region media.
Delta Financial agreed to pay \$12 million to settle investigations by
the New York State Department of Banking and New York State attorney
general Eliot Spitzer. It also reached a settlement with the U.S.
Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, and the U.S.
Department of Housing and Urban Development. In an interview with
<span class="italic">Newsday</span>, Delta’s chief executive said: “The
concept of us giving a loan to someone who is mentally challenged would
make absolutely no business sense, never mind the ethics involved.” See
Ron Howell and R<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.7.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>andi Feigenbaum, “Customers, Attorney General
Say Mortgage Firm Uses Unfair Tactics,”
<span class="italic">Newsday</span>, Oct. 31, 1999.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Lehman took an ownership interest:</span> Lehman
started Finance America in 1999 and took its initial stake in BNC in
2000.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the only game”:</span> Brian Chisick’s
testimony in <span class="italic">FTC v. First Alliance</span>. Lehman
never exercised the stock warrants.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>First National Bank of Keystone:</span> See note
on page 313, <span class="italic">“Keystone knew nothing,”</span> for
citations on the history of Keystone’s rise and fall.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA317.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Under Lehman’s guidance:</span> Lehman
eventually backed away from Keystone, cutting back on the size of a
later transaction and then not doing business with the bank for
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page332"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA318"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA318.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA318.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>roughly two years. However, according to
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA318.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA318.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">National Mortgage
News</span>, Lehman eventually rekindled the relationship, putting
together a \$350 million securitization for the bank in December 1998.
It canceled the securitization after it became clear that turmoil in the
financial markets had made such deals “cost-prohibitive,” the trade
paper said. “Keystone was working on a deal with Lehman Brothers in
December, but the pricing just got out of hand and they bagged it,” an
industry source told the paper. See “High-LTV Securitizations Tail Off,”
<span class="italic">National Mortgage News</span>, Jan. 29, 1999.

<span class="italic">The</span> New York Times <span class="italic">was
working on a story:</span> Bill Ahearn’s

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA318.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Citigroup and subprime:</span> See especially
Michael Hudson, “Banking on Misery,” <span class="italic">Southern
Exposure</span>, Summer 2003. Citi claimed it bought Associates with the
intention of cleaning up the lender’s abuses by folding it into its
existing subprime unit, CitiFinancial. But CitiFinancial had its own
record of bad practices, and the newly combined subprime operations
continued to gouge and exploit vulnerable consumers—targeting, one loan
officer testified, anyone who “appeared uneducated, inarticulate, was a
minority, or was particularly young or old.” The
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page333"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA319"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA319.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA319.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>idea that Citigroup was interested in cleaning
up a flawed company is also belied by this historical fact: Citi chief
executive Sanford “Sandy” Weill had been involved in dicey subprime
enterprises for nearly a decade and a half before the Associates
acquisition. He had used a Baltimore-based subprime lender, Commercial
Credit, as the platform for building the financial empire that provided
him the cash and clout to take over Citi, and Commercial Credit had
become the target of many lawsuits alleging lending abuses during the
Weill era. In an interview for the <span class="italic">Southern
Exposure</span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA319.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> article, a former Commercial Credit manager in
Mississippi recalled that, under Weill, employees were pressured to meet
quotas for generating loans and selling costly insurance—and to use
slick talk to prevent customers from understanding what they were
getting. “Over a period of time,” he said, “it went from a family,
employee-oriented company—doing the right thing, trying to help its
customers—to this cutthroat thing of anything that will get us more
business.”

class="calibre2"></span>Ameriquest, ACORN, and the FTC:</span> See Mike

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.0.0.1"

<span class="italic">According to Kas: Kas v. The DDB Needham Worldwide

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.3.0"

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.8.0"

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Kuhn was certainly motivated:</span> Extensive
interviews with Stephen Kuhn, a former Ameriquest loan officer. See also
<span class="italic">Kuhn v. Ameriquest</span>, U.S. District Court for
the District of Kansas, 2004, a wrongful dismissal lawsuit that claimed
Kuhn was fired after he complained about Ameriquest’s unethical
practices. Others who worked with Kuhn in Ameriquest’s Leawood, Kansas,
office, including Rob Hurtig and Brien Hanley, gave similar accounts of
the practices in the branch. “The stuff you’re asked to do, just to
close files, was sick,” Hurtig said. He said workers falsified documents
and ta<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.9.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>rgeted vulnerable borrowers for “the shittiest
deals possible.” He said he quit after a few months because “it’s really
hard to sell people things when you know you’re screwing them.” Hanley
said Ameriquest pressured would-be borrowers “to do it now, to do it
right this second, so they couldn’t shop around” and find better deals
elsewhere. Falsification of documents, he said, “was just common
practice. If you were trying to get a loan done, that’s what you did.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Armon Williams:</span> I interviewed Armon
Williams, a former Ameriquest employee, for a story in the
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times.</span> See Mike Hudson and E.
Scott Reckard, “Workers Say Lender Ran ‘Boiler Rooms,’”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Feb. 4, 2005. Like many
others at Ameriquest, Williams was a mortgage-industry neophyte who
didn’t fully understand until later how Ameriquest’s tactics hurt
consumers. He said he felt regret for some of the things he had done.
When I contacted him again in 2009, he declined to discuss his
experiences further. He said he didn’t want to revisit that time in his
life.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the worst case scenario”:</span> Interview with
Jason DeBruler, a former Ameriquest employee.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA320.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“dual purpose of both making sure the
loan”:</span> Sept. 23, 2004, affidavit of Joseph Khaliq, who worked for
Ameriquest in Santa Clara and Campbell, California, in
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page335"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Landa v. Ameriquest</span>, U.S. District Court
for the Northern District of California, 2003.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Loan officers pressured appraisers:</span> For
our Feb. 4, 2005, <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span> article,
Scott Reckard and I interviewed Michael Filip and appraisers in five
other state<span class="bold1">s</span>, all of whom described
Ameriquest’s strong-arm tactics. Ameriquest told us it had “tight
controls and policies to help ensure accurate property valuations.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Christopher J. Warren:</span> Warren’s personal
written statement, which is attached to a Feb. 4, 2009, affidavit by an
IRS criminal investigator in support of an arrest warrant for Warren in
<span class="italic">USA v. Warren</span>, U.S. District Court for the
Eastern District of California, Case \# 2:09-mj-00046-KJM-1. The bank
fraud charges in that case were later dropped in favor of charges of
money laundering and other counts, Case \# 2:09-cr-00121-FCD. None of
these charges involved his work at Ameriquest.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Aryan Nation”:</span> Interviews with Todd
Strobel and Michael Bischoff, former Ameriquest employees, and documents
in employment discrimination cases filed against Ameriquest, including
Strobel’s March 6, 2003, deposition in <span class="italic">In re: Tom
Reed and Ameriquest Mortgage</span>, American Arbitration Association
proceeding, and the complaint in <span class="italic">Theriot v.
Ameriquest</span>, Orange County Superior Court, 2006. See also Kevin
Lynch, “Fired Worker Says Employer Discriminated,”
<span class="italic">Detroit News</span>, Oct. 13, 2000.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Wendell Raphael:</span> Interview with Wendell
Raphael, a longtime mortgage executive. Raphael told me that he
frequently fielded calls from appraisers who said they were being
pressured by branch employees to inflate home values; in some cases, the
appraisers told him, they were owed thousands of dollars for work they’d
done for the company, but the money was being held hostage until they
agreed to “hit the value” on a pending assignment. Raphael also heard
from “pissed-off” borrowers. They claimed they’d been lied to, that
documents had been forged, and that they’d been stuck with
outl<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>andish fees. He challenged them: “Do you have
proof?” Most said: “What’s your fax number?” The documentation they sent
often satisfied him that they were telling the truth. I interviewed
Raphael shortly before his death. In response to my questions about
Raphael’s statements to me, Ameriquest said: “Mr. Raphael was a longtime
employee of the Company who passed away. We have no knowledge of Mr.
Raphael ever making statements similar to the ones you have alleged. Nor
are we aware of Mr. Raphael ever raising these issues with anyone at the
Company. In fact, we are troubled that your only
Com<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.4.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>pany source is a deceased former executive who
during his many years of employment had no prior history of making any
statements similar to the ones you allege. Regardless, your assertions
are simply not accurate.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>They were ordering appraisal after
appraisal:</span> Barry Bates, who worked briefly as Ameriquest’s chief
appraiser in the early 2000s, confirmed that questionable appraisals
were a problem at the lender. He told me he ran into problems with
management when he tried to cull dishonest appraisers from Ameriquest’s
approved list. The sales force saw him as “the enemy,” he said. “As soon
as I removed one bad appraiser from the list, they put somebody new on”
who was just as bad. When he tried to raise the issue with senior
executives, he said, he got “a look that I’ll never forget. It was
calm<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA321.w.1.5.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>, cool, and collected, but the look said: You
are history.” Soon <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page336"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>after, he said, he was called in by a human
resources staffer and told he was being let go. The reason: “loss of
confidence” in his work.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="bold1">9. The Battle for Georgia</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Our goal is to allow thrifts”:</span> Quoted in
Binyamin Appelbaum and Ellen Nakashima, “Banking Regulator Played
Advocate over Enforcer,” <span class="italic">Washington Post</span>,
Nov. 23, 2008. See also a policy brief prepared by the Center for
Responsible Lending, “Neglect and Inaction: An Analysis of Federal
Banking Regulators’ Failure to Enforce Consumer Protections,” July 13,
2009, <span class="xrefURL"><a
href="http://www.responsiblelending.org/mortgage-lending/policy-legislation/regulators/regulators-failure-to-enforce-consumer-protections.html"
class="calibre6">http://www.responsiblelending.org/mortgage-lending/policy-legislation/regulators/regulators-failure-to-enforce-consumer-protections.html</a></span>.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>involving small Texas banks:</span> Testimony of
John C. Dugan, “Improving Federal Consumer Protection in Financial
Services,” Hearing Before the House Committee on Financial services,
June 13, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We cannot intercede”:</span> Greg Ip and Damian
Paletta, “Lending Oversight: Regulators Scrutinized in Mortgage
Meltdown; States, Federal Agencies Clashed on subprimes as Market
Ballooned,” <span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, Mar. 22,
2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“regulatory capture”:</span> Federal banking
regulators tended to accept the financial industry’s argument that
consumer protection rules are a drag on banks, cutting into their bottom
line and thus endangering their “safety and soundness.” Actually, the
opposite has proven to be true. Consumer protection helps prevent
reckless business practices that can end in disaster not only for the
customers but also for banks and their shareholders. As FDIC chairman
Sheila Bair has said, “Protecting the consumer from…perils is not simply
a do-good public service. In fact, consumer protection and safe and
sound<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.5.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> lending practices are two sides of the same
coin. Lenders who put their retail customers at risk also put
themselves, their investors, and our entire financial system in danger.”
In particular, if borrowers can’t afford their loans, the resulting
foreclosures will cause losses for banks, threatening their safety.
Sheila C. Bair, “The Future of Mortgage Finance,” remarks at the 2008
annual meeting of the National Association for Business Economics,
Washington, D.C., Oct. 6, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“no evidence of predatory lending”:</span> See
the OCC fact sheet, “Preemption Determination and Order Concerning the
Georgia Fair Lending Act: Questions and Answers,” July 31, 2003.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>National City Mortgage:</span> Eric Nalder,
“Mortgage System Crumbled While Regulators Jousted,”
<span class="italic">Seattle Post-Intelligencer</span>, Oct. 11, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“They let Citigroup off”:</span> Interview with
Matthew Lee, director of Fair Finance Watch, a New York City–based
watchdog group. For more on Citigroup and the FTC settlement, see
Michael Hudson, “Banking on Misery,” <span class="italic">Southern
Exposure</span>, Summer 2003.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Cross report on Household International:</span>
Interview with Chuck Cross, former director of consumer services for the
Department of Financial Institutions, Washington State, and various news
articles. See in particular Brian Collins, “State Regulator Slams
Household Practices,” <span class="italic">National Mortgage
News</span>, Sept. 2, 2002.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA322.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“These guys are criminals”:</span> Interview

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA325.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Boiler Room training video:</span> Interviews

<span class="italic">Boiler Room</span>…a movie
depict<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA325.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>ing aggressive telephone sales tactics used to

r<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA325.w.1.7.0.1"

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA325.w.1.9.0"

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA325.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“Omar did ten”:</span> Interview with Omar Ross.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA325.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>in everyone’s best interest if Kuhn and
Ameriquest parted:</span> Stephen Kuhn decided to sue Ameriquest for

rich <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page340"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>and too powerful. He sued anyway, representing
himself and filing a handwritten legal complaint, alleging that he had
been fired because “I stated…that Ameriquest’s fees, rates & business
ethics were terrible.” See
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Kuhn v. Ameriquest</span>,
U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas, 2004. A judge ordered

and his lawsuit was dismissed for good in 2006.

<span class="italic">Mark Glover’s wrongful termination lawsuit: Glover
v. Ameriquest</span>, Orange County Superior Court, 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Christopher J. Warren, the mortgage
fraudster:</span> Warren’s personal written statement attached to the
