Warren,</span> U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of
California, Case \#
2:09-mj-00046-KJ<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>M-1.

<span class="italic">New Century:</span> James R. Hagerty, Ruth Simon,
Michael Corkery, and Gregory Zuckerman, “Home Stretch: At a Mortgage
Lender, Rapid Rise, Faster Fall,” <span class="italic">Wall Street
Journal</span>, Mar. 12, 2007; and John Gittelsohn and Matthew Padilla,
“Cutting-Edge Company to Cautionary Tale,” <span class="italic">Orange
County Register</span>, Apr. 19, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We were basically the black sheep”:</span>
David Heath, “At Top Subprime Mortgage Lender, Policies Were Invitation
to Fraud,” Huffington Post Investigative Fund, Dec. 12, 2009. The
borrowers who went after Long Beach in court included Luis Mapula and
Cristina Plata, a Latino couple from East San Jose, California, who
claimed they had been saddled with a complex, unaffordable loan package
after the lender approved an application that falsely claimed the family
had an income of more than \$100,000, as well as \$19,700 in the bank, a
\$22,000 Acura, and \$28,000 in furniture and personal
property.<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> The loan papers called for the family to
initially pay over \$3,500 a month, more than their actual take-home
pay. Things would only get worse: the monthly payments were poised to
adjust every six months and climb to \$4,300 and beyond. Without
admitting wrongdoing, Long Beach and the other firms involved in the
deal settled the lawsuit for \$250,000. See Pete Carey, “The Harsh Side
of the Housing Boom,” <span class="italic">Mercury News</span>, Mar. 11,
2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“They were just nasty products”:</span> Drew
DeSilver, “Reckless Strategies Doomed WaMu,”
<span class="italic">Seattle Times</span>, Oct. 25, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The two moguls met:</span> Paul Muolo and Mathew
Padilla, <span class="italic">Chain of Blame: How Wall Street Caused the
Mortgage and Credit Crisis</span> (Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons,
2008), pp. 73–74, 87, and 95. See also E. Scott Reckard and Jim
Puzzanghera, “SEC Suit Accuses Mozilo of Fraud,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, June 5, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>When Countrywide sold prime loans:</span>
Gretchen Morgenson, “Inside the Countrywide Lending Spree,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Aug. 26, 2007. Figures are
for 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It was Roland’s baby”:</span> Interview with
Terry Rouch, a former wholesale loan officer at Argent Mortgage.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Elizabeth Redrick’s complaint:</span> Mark
Gillespie, “Argent Lender Found Biased Against Blacks,”
<span class="italic">Cleveland Plain Dealer</span>, Mar. 19, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA326.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Kramer charged that Argent had colluded</span>:
Wells Fargo’s relationship with Argent in Cleveland was not an anomaly.
Government lawsuits alleged that Wells Fargo’s mortgage operations were
driven by a sales culture where profiteering and discrimination went
hand in hand. In court papers, one former employee recalled
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page341"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>coworkers calling minority customers “mud
people,” describing mortgages in minority neighborhoods as “ghetto
loans,” and justifying putting minorities into high-priced mortgages by
saying, “Those people don’t pay their bills.” Wells Fargo aggressively
sold subprime loans to black homeowners by building alliances with
influential figures in the black community. Its Affinity Group Marketing
unit targeted black churches, trying to use pastors’ sway over their
flocks to help the company sell loans. The bank also teamed with Tavis
Smiley, one of the nation’s most influential African-American
author<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>s and talk-show hosts. Smiley was the keynote
speaker at “Wealth Building” seminars that the banking giant held in
predominantly black neighborhoods in Baltimore, Chicago, and other
cities. Wells Fargo had representatives on-site to meet with audience
members afterward, using the events to lure them into subprime
mortgages, according to a lawsuit filed by Illinois’s attorney general.
(In a written statement, Smiley acknowledged that he had partnered with
Wells Fargo on wealth-building initiatives. He said, though, that he had
not been a “spokesperson or representative” for Wells
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.0.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>Fargo and pointed out that many African-American
and Latino national civil rights organizations had had similar
relationships with the bank. “In this economic climate we continue to be
reminded every day that there is no perfect company,” he wrote, adding
that he supported “any official and credible investigation of
allegations of any company accused of disrespecting communities of color
with discriminatory practices.”)\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span> See affidavits by Elizabeth M. Jacobson and
Tony Paschal in <span class="italic">Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
v. Wells Fargo Bank</span>, U.S. District Court for the District of
Maryland, 2008, documents 74-16 and 74-17; <span class="italic">People
of the State of Illinois v. Wells Fargo and Company</span>, Cook County
(Ill.) Circuit Court, 2009; and Mary Kane, “Suit Alleges Trusted Blacks
Drew Minorities to High-Rate Loans,” <span class="italic">Washington
Indepen dent</span>, Sept. 17, 2009.

<span class="italic">He had received roughly \$500,000:</span> Figures
based on author’s analysis of data at
<span class="xrefURL"><a href="http://OpenSecrets.org" class="calibre6">OpenSecrets.org</a></span>,
a service of the Center for Responsive Politics that tracks
f<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>ederal campaign data.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Responsible Lending Act:</span> Background on
this bill comes from Richard Lord, <span class="italic">American
Nightmare: Predatory Lending and the Foreclosure of the American
Dream</span> (Monroe, Me.: Common Courage Press, 2004), pp. 194–97.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I think that everyone in this room
agrees”:</span> Ney’s words and other remarks from the hearing come from
a Federal Document Clearing House transcript of House Committee on
Financial Services, Subcommittees on Financial Institutions and Consumer
Credit and on Housing and Community Opportunity, Hearing on “Protecting
Homeowners: Preventing Abusive Lending While Preserving Access to
Credit,” Nov. 5, 2003.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>New Century had finished a distant
second:</span> Citigroup and Household ranked third and fourth, both
recording just over \$20 billion in subprime loan volume.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The industry’s overall loan volume topped \$330
billion:</span> Bernard Condon, “Till Debt Do Us Part,”
<span class="italic">Forbes</span>, Feb. 16, 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA327.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“They’re on fire right now”:</span> Paul Muolo,
“Did Ameriquest Earn \$1B Last Year?” <span class="italic">National
Mortgage News</span>, Apr. 5, 2004.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page342" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>12. Chimera</span>

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">Cedric Washington:</span> This account is based on
Washington’s complaint in <span class="italic">Washington v. Finance
America</span>, Sacramento County Superior Court, 2005. Lehman Brothers
said Washington’s lawsuit “had no merit” and was “not brought in good
faith.” The lawsuit was settled in 2006 on undisclosed terms.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>BNC and Finance America employees:</span> I
investigated BNC and Finance America as a reporter for the
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>. See Michael Hudson,
“Lending a Hand: How Wall Street Stoked the Mortgage Meltdown,”
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, June 27, 2007. I
collected accounts from twenty-five former BNC and Finance America
employees who stated that questionable loans and falsified paperwork
were a problem. Most were on the record and specified in detail the bad
practices they witnessed. It should be noted that five other former
employees told me that the companies had run a tight ship, at least in
the offices <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>where they worked. They said the lenders had
good fraud controls in place and worked to screen out dicey loans. “We
didn’t just push things through,” Barbara Webb, who worked for Finance
America and BNC in Texas in 2004 and 2005, told me. “Everything we did
was by the guidelines.” Lehman was vehement that everything was on the
up-and-up at its subprime origination platforms. It questioned the
credibility of the former employees who criticized the lenders’
practices, noting that many of them had never said anything about fraud
while they worked for the companies. Lehman said its
employees<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.2.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span> were committed to “the highest standards of
governance and ethical behavior.” The weight of the evidence from former
employees’ statements and from borrowers’ lawsuits, however, led me to
conclude that fraud and reckless sales policies were serious problems at
BNC and Finance America. Kendra Eckhart worked as an underwriter in
BNC’s Roseville, Minnesota, branch. Employees who tried to stop
questionable loans, she said, got verbal lashings from salespeople and
managers: “Are you going to blow the deal over this?” Little else
mattered but selling loans. “You sacrifice everything, really, to get
v<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.2.0.3"
class="calibre2"></span>olume,” Eckhart said. Upper management rarely
backed the underwriters, she said; usually sales won and the loans were
eventually pushed through. The accounts collected from employees were
supported by those provided in court records by borrowers who alleged
their loans had been pushed through via falsified paperwork and other
unseemly tactics.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>BNC’s Sacramento branch:</span> The lawsuit,
filed by Coleen Colombo and five other women who worked at the branch,
claimed that managers punished employees for reporting fraud and allowed
sexual harassment to flourish at the branch. For a 2007 article in the
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, I interviewed eight
women who had worked in the office, including five of the six plaintiffs
in the suit against BNC. The details of their allegations are also
described in Mara Der Hovanesian, “Sex, Lies, and subprime Mortgages,”
<span class="italic">BusinessWeek</span>, Nov. 13, 2008, as well as in
the television report “Mortgage Company
Employe<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA328.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>es Claim Harassment,” KCRA, Sept. 7, 2005,
<span class="xrefURL"><a href="http://www.ksbw.com/news/4946507/detail.html"
class="calibre6">http://www.ksbw.com/news/4946507/detail.html</a></span>,
and <span class="italic">Colombo et al. v. BNC Mortgage Inc.</span>,
Sacramento Superior Court, 2005. The <span class="italic">Colombo</span>
case was put on hold due to Lehman’s bankruptcy filing in late 2008. In
a statement in 2007, Lehman said: “The factual context for the events in
Sacramento reflects the seriousness with which we take allegations of
fraud…. With regard to the allegations made by six
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page343"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>former employees in the pending lawsuit, we also
have reviewed them thoroughly and are confident that they are baseless
and without merit.”

<span class="italic">“contributed to the highest homeownership”:</span>
Testimony of Stephen W. Prough, chairman, Ameriquest Mortgage Company,
before the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs,
Washington, D.C., July 26, 2001.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In 2004, just one-quarter of 1 percent of its
mortgages:</span> Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data for 2004 show that
Ameriquest made 177,806 refinancing loans, 17,303 home-improvement loans
and 492 home-purchase loans.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Best estimates were that less than 10
percent:</span> Center for Responsible Lending, “subprime Lending: A Net
Drain on Homeownership,” Mar. 27, 2007. This ground-breaking study found
that 62 percent of subprime mortgages during the period from 1998 to
2006 were refinancings. Of the remainder, the study found, roughly 9
percent were for first-time home purchases and another 29 percent went
to current homeowners who were buying another house (either to replace
their current home, as a second home, or as an investment). The study
estimated that subprime loans made in 2005 produced fewer than 225,000
new<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> homeowners, but would result in more than half
a million foreclosures, mostly from unaffordable refinance loans.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“foundation of healthy communities”:</span>
Quoted in an Ameriquest press release.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Duane and Gertrude O’Connor:</span> Documents in
<span class="italic">Duane and Gertrude Connor v. Ameriquest et
al.</span>, U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, 2007,
including the August 10, 2007, complaint and the January 16, 2007,
affidavits from Gertrude and Duane O’Connor.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In addition to Deutsche Bank:</span> As of 2005,
Deutsche Bank and Morgan Stanley had the biggest lines of credit in
place for Arnall’s companies, at \$3 billion apiece. JPMorgan Chase and
Merrill were close behind, at roughly \$2.8 billion each. Citigroup
maintained a \$1.85 billion line of credit for Arnall’s lenders. These
figures are based on ACC Capital Holdings’ “Consolidated Financial
Statements” for the three years ending December 31, 2005. Lehman
Brothers didn’t provide a line of credit to ACC; it provided funding to
Ameriquest by buying the lender’s loans and then wrapping them into
Lehman<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.5.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>’s own securitizations.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The O’Connors’ mortgage was one of more than
eighty-five hundred:</span> Documents filed with securities regulators
regarding Ameriquest Mortgage Securities Inc. Asset-Backed Pass-Through
Certificates, Series 2004-R11, including the November 2004 Prospectus
Supplement and Form 8K, Dec. 30, 2004, Exhibit 99.2, “Characteristics of
the Mortgage Pool.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>2004-R11 securitization techniques:</span>
“Moody’s Rates Ameriquest’s 2004-R11 Deal Aaa,” Moody’s Investors
service press release, Nov. 29, 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch:</span> Elliot Blair
Smith, “Bringing Down Wall Street as Ratings Let Loose Subprime
Scourge,” Bloomberg News, Sept. 24, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA329.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>2004-R11 investors:</span> Information from
Bloomberg and <span class="italic">Mutual Fund Prospectus
Express</span>. The firms purchased the mortgage-backed securities
through various investment funds they sponsored, such as the JPMorgan
Global Strategic Income Fund and Citigroup’s Smith Barney Diversified
Strategic Income Fund. Fidelity appeared to be one of the most active
buyers of securities from the deal. Investments
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page344"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>in the deal ended up in the Fidelity Investment
Grade Bond Fund, Fidelity Inflation Protected Bond Fund, Fidelity
Tactical Income Central Fund, Fidelity VIP Investment Grade Central
Investment Portfolio, and so on.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">“Eager to scrape the X-rated mud”:</span> Bruce
Horovitz, “Ameriquest Places Super Bet,” <span class="italic">USA
Today</span>, Oct. 7, 2004.

<span class="italic">Progress for America Voter Fund:</span> Jeanne
Cummings, “Republicans Tap Rich Donors to Form Group Targeting Kerry,”
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, Aug. 25, 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>National Mortgage News floated a story:</span>
Paul Muolo, “Ameriquest Looks at IPO,” <span class="italic">National
Mortgage News</span>, Dec. 20, 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>the third-largest IPO:</span> “The Biggest U.S.
IPOs Ever,” <span class="italic">BusinessWeek</span> online,
<span class="xrefURL"><a href="http://images.businessweek.com/ss/06/10/us_ipos/index_01.htm"
class="calibre6">http://images.businessweek.com/ss/06/10/us_ipos/index_01.htm</a></span>.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>13. The Investigators</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Ed Parker:</span> Multiple interviews with Ed
Parker, former fraud investigation manager at Ameriquest; testimony by
Parker and Ameriquest executives in <span class="italic">Parker v.
Ameriquest</span>, American Arbitration Association, 2007; and Parker’s
June 9, 2008, deposition in <span class="italic">Ricci v.
Ameriquest</span>, Hennepin County (Minn.) District Court, 2005.\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span> In a written response to my questions, the
company said, “Mr. Parker is not a credible source, according to an
independent arbitrator who evaluated Mr. Parker’s allegations against
the Company.” Parker did lose his wrongful dismissal claim against the
company. The arbitrator wrote that Parker didn’t prove the elements of
his claim: “Virtually the only evidence pointing to discrimination by
Ameriquest against him is his own unsubstantiated conclusory opinion.”
It should be noted, however, that the arbitrator didn’t hear from other
former Ameriquest employees who shared Parker’s view that
th<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.6.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>e company didn’t aggressively move to stamp out
fraud, and encouraged employees to do whatever it took to book loans. It
should be noted, too, that the arbitrator also wrote: “One can agree
that Mr. Parker was not treated as well by Ameriquest as he might have
been, or should have been. He had been a good and trusted employee, and
there is no criticism of his performance as a fraud investigator.”\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span> Besides, whether he was wrongfully fired or
demoted didn’t go to the heart of the issue that Parker’s account in
this book raises; it was hard for him to find a legal hook on which to
hang claims that he was marginalized and that various personnel moves
and reorganizations helped discourage aggressive investigation of fraud.
Because California is an “at will” employment state, the arbitrator
added, employees such as Parker could be “terminated at any given time
for any ordinary reason.” Parker’s dismissal came in 2006 as Ameriquest
was closing its branch offices across the nation and
he<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA330.w.1.7.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> was among the thousands of employees who were
laid off. That made it hard to determine whether he had been fired in
retaliation for his investigative work or simply as part of the bigger
staff purge.

<span class="italic">“You’re like a dog on a leash”:</span> Interview
with Kelly J. Dragna, who worked at Ameriquest from 2002 to 2006 as an
internal auditor and fraud analyst, joining Ed Parker’s team in 2005.
For the fraudsters inside the company, Dragna said, it was a bit like
driving seventy-five miles per hour in a sixty-five-mile-per-hour zone.
Some might get pulled over and penalized, but most zoomed by without a
care. <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page345"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Managers preferred to look the other way. “There
was never an attempt to send a message that they wouldn’t tolerate
this,” Dragna said. “It was just: ‘You get caught, you’re on your own.’
The company wasn’t really totally opposed to the fraud. They were
willing to tolerate it as long as you didn’t get caught.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Ameriquest’s new and improved standards:</span>
In a September 25, 2003, Ameriquest press release, several leaders in
politics and community organizing praised the companies’ updated “best
practices.” Sheila Bair, a former assistant secretary of the Treasury
(and later head of the FDIC), called Ameriquest’s revised list “the most
progressive set of lender best practices I have ever seen. Three cheers
for Ameriquest for leading the industry.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“You can either make the sale or you can make
the disclosure”:</span> Interview with David Huey, assistant attorney
general, Washington State.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The two sides mingled before dinner:</span> The
account of the dinner is based on interviews with David Huey, Chuck
Cross, Prentiss Cox, Tom James, and Ben Diehl, an assistant attorney
general of California. See also the transcript of the May 9, 2007,
deposition of former ACC Capital chief executive Wayne Lee in
<span class="italic">In Re: Ameriquest Mortgage Co. Mortgage Lending
Practices Litigation</span>, U.S. District Court for the Northern
District of Illinois, MDL No. 1715, Lead Case No. 05-cv-07097, pp.
95–96.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>14. The Big Game</span>

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>American Nightmare: Rich’s book was published in
the fall of 2004. It reflected his deep reporting—sifting through court
records and knocking on doors in and around Pittsburgh—as well as his
prescient analysis of how Wall Street was fueling abusive lending. See
Rich Lord, <span class="italic">American Nightmare: Predatory Lending
and the Foreclosure of the American Dream</span> (Monroe, Me.: Common
Courage Press, 2004).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>dozens of lawsuits:</span> Following up on one
of the cases in PACER, I talked to Nate McKitterick, the attorney for a
woman from East Palo Alto, California, who was suing the company. She
claimed that Ameriquest employees tricked her into signing a mortgage
that required her to pay \$2,494 a month, more than she was earning
cleaning houses. All the negotiations were in Spanish, McKitterick said,
but all the loan documents were in English—a language she could not
speak or read. “The only thing she ever got from Ameriquest that was in
Spanish was a foreclosure notice,” he said. See Mike Hudson and
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.6.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>E. Scott Reckard, “Workers Say Lender Ran
‘Boiler Rooms,’” <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Feb. 4,
2005, and <span class="italic">Landa v. Ameriquest</span>, U.S. District
Court for the Northern District of California, 2003.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I couldn’t live with myself”:</span> Interview
with Gilbert Stansell, who worked for just two months—May and June
2004—at Ameriquest’s Grand Rapids branch. He said he was fired for lack
of production.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA331.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We just couldn’t take it”:</span> Interview
with Caleb Conklin, who worked for Ameriquest from October 2003 to
August 2004 at its Grand Rapids branch. Conklin was part of the group
that helped reopen the Grand Rapids office after Ed Parker had helped
clean house there. “It just felt like it just wasn’t right,” Conklin
said. “They’re making us sell and sell, but we’re not pitching good
deals.” The fees on Ameriquest’s loans were twice what borrowers could
have gotten at other lenders, Conklin said.\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page346"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>One of Conklin’s coworkers at the branch was
Jason DeBruler. During his eleven months at Ameriquest, DeBruler said,
he realized that borrowers were “lied to all the way up to the day of
closing as to what the closing costs were.” He said management told loan
officers to reveal only \$1,500 of the closing costs, and to not mention
the \$3,000 to \$5,000 most borrowers were charged in up-front points.
He said inflated appraisals continued to be a problem at the Grand
Rapids branch, long after the branch was shut down and reopened with a
fresh staff. The branch would pay appraisers a bonus
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>on top of their regular fee so long as they
would “come in with the value that we need.”

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.0.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">Lawsuits in St. Louis and Alabama: Rednour et al.
v. Ameriquest</span>, U.S. District Court for Eastern District of
Missouri, 2004; <span class="italic">Powell et al. v. Ameriquest,</span>
U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Alabama, 2004.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“a couple may come out bad”:</span> Rodrigo J.
Alba, Ameriquest’s vice president for federal and regulatory affairs,
was quoted in David Feldheim, “Subprime Lenders Ameriquest Eyes Prime
Mortgage Market,” Dow Jones Newswires, Mar. 11, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>three women in Tampa:</span> E. Scott Reckard
and Mike Hudson, “Doubt Is Cast on Loan Papers,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, Mar. 28, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>more than \$2.7 billion:</span> ACC Capital
Holdings’ “Consolidated Financial Statements” for the three years ending
December 31, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“As we reflect on the evolution of consumer
credit”:</span> Alan Greenspan, “Consumer Finance,” remarks at the
Fourth Annual Community Affairs Research Conference, Federal Reserve
System, Washington, D.C., Apr. 8, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the impression that there were a lot”:</span>
Edmund L. Andrews, “Fed Shrugged as subprime Crisis Spread,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Dec. 18, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“He just wasn’t interested”:</span> Ibid.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Other watchdog groups that had benefited:</span>
Mike Hudson, “Ameriquest’s Ties to Watchdog Groups Are Tested,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, May 22, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.9.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“six to eight times oversubscribed”:</span>
Grant Catton, “Ameriquest Unscathed by Legal Woes,”
<span class="italic">Asset Securitization Report</span>, Feb. 28, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.10.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“replete with questionable loans”:</span>
Kathleen C. Engel and Patricia A. McCoy, “Turning a Blind Eye: Wall
Street Finance of Predatory Lending,” <span class="italic">Fordham Law
Review</span> 75 (2007), p. 2041.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.11.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“your heads are buried in cash”:</span>
Interview with Prentiss Cox. Subprime had become “more or less a pirate
industry,” he said. “It was just plunder and take everything you can
today.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.12.0"
class="calibre2"></span>the real culprits:</span> There was little doubt
that professional fraudsters were targeting the mortgage industry,
taking advantage of lenders’ lax underwriting standards and the go-go
exuberance of the housing boom. In Dayton, Ohio, for example, ABN Amro
Mortgage Group Inc. reported that it lost \$2 million after a convicted
felon and other conspirators arranged as many as twenty-three mortgages
in the names of dead people. Chip Burrus, assistant director of the
FBI’s criminal investigative division, noted that criminal gangs
involved in drug dealing and other street crimes had branched into
m<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA332.w.1.12.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>ortgage fraud. “It’s more profitable and less
risky,” he said. See James R. Hagerty and Michael Hudson, “Town’s
Residents Say They Were Targets of Big Mortgage Fraud,”
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, Sept. 28, 2006.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page347" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It is a serious, and sometimes
criminal”:</span> Letter from Jonathan L. Kempner, president and CEO of
the Mortgage Bankers Association, dated Apr. 1, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Many borrowers had no idea:</span> Many of the
mortgage professionals I interviewed said borrowers were, more often
than not, unaware that information had been falsified to push their
loans through. Scott Montilla, a former IndyMac mortgage underwriter in
Arizona, confirmed to me that many borrowers were not aware that their
stated incomes were being inflated during the application process: “A
lot of times you talked to the customer and the customer said: ‘I never
told them I made that much.’” The case of Ben Butler, an eighty-year-old
retiree in Savannah, Georgia, is instructive on this
poi<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>nt. Butler secured a loan from IndyMac in 2005
to build a modular house. IndyMac approved the mortgage based on an
application that said Butler made \$3,825 a month in Social Security
income. The only problem: the maximum Social Security benefit at the
time was barely half that. Butler had no idea his income had been
inflated by IndyMac or the mortgage broker who arranged the deal, his
attorney maintained. Even if IndyMac wasn’t the one that puffed up the
dollar figure, the attorney said, it should have caught such an obvious
lie. In a letter to IndyMac, the attorney argued that the income listed
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.1.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>in his client’s application paperwork “was not
provided by Mr. Butler and was a complete fabrication by someone ‘in the
loop’ so to speak. The mortgage broker and IndyMac are two of the
persons/entities in that loop…. There is no amount of income filled in
on the original application. Mr. Butler was never asked to state his
income. Any prudent underwriter should have questioned the income
considering the amount/source and required proof.” See Mike Hudson,
“IndyMac: What Went Wrong? How an ‘Alt-A’ Leader Fueled Its Growth with
Unsound and Abusive Mortgage Lending,” Center for Responsible
Lendin<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.1.0.3"
class="calibre2"></span>g, June 30, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“if the housing bubble burst”:</span> This is
not an exercise in hindsight. Prentiss Cox said exactly that in
telephone discussions with me in the second half of 2005, after he was
free to talk generally about his concerns about the subprime market:
“Ultimately, these pools are much more risky than the people who are
investing in them think they are. These pools have been created almost
completely in the context of an unprecedented rise in home values.
Imagine what happens if the housing bubble bursts.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>It was far less than what Household:</span> For
Roland Arnall, it was a relief to attach a dollar figure to his
company’s exposure. After spending years in a single-minded effort to
build his fortune, Arnall was now spending more and more time trying to
protect his wealth from those who wanted a piece of it. To reduce the
tax bite from the IRS, he had poured much of his money—more than \$1
billion—into oil and gas exploration, a venture that he hoped would be
both a tax shelter and a new profit center. In the summer of 2005,
Arnall also found himself fighting a battle closer to home.
Hi<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA333.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>s first wife, Sally, had filed to reopen their
divorce case, suggesting that he had cheated her out of tens of millions
or even hundreds of millions of dollars. “I believe I was misled and
that I received substantially less than my share of the financial empire
we amassed during our marriage,” she said in a court filing. For all his
secrecy, he had been unable to hide his newfound wealth from his
ex-wife. Sally said she had first learned how big Roland’s business
operations were when she <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page348"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>saw the November 2004 issue of
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Forbes</span>, which placed
his fortune at \$2 billion. The case was settled on undisclosed terms.
<span class="italic">In Re: Marriage of Arnall</span>, Los Angeles
Superior Court, filed in 1996 and reopened in 2005; and Scott Reckard,
“Ex-Wife of Loan Exec Asks for Probe,” <span class="italic">Los Angeles
Times</span>, Aug. 22, 2005.

<span class="italic">“Their words were not so much heard as
acclaimed”:</span> Lawrence G. McDonald with Patrick Robinson,
<span class="italic">A Colossal Failure of Common Sense: The Inside
Story of the Collapse of Lehman Brothers</span> (New York: Crown
Business, 2009). See especially pp. 106–13 and 125–38.

<span class="italic">McCarthy believed Dick Fuld:</span> Larry McCarthy
told <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>Reuters he quit Lehman after repeatedly warning
that the firm was too leveraged on borrowed money and the real-estate
market couldn’t keep going up forever. For his part, Fuld denied that he
had isolated himself from those who tried to warn him of the risks the
company was taking on: “I left my office, I left my office plenty.”
Clare Baldwin, Jui Chakrovorty, and Jonathan Spicer, “Fuld Says Being
‘Dumped On’ for Lehman Failure,” Reuters, Sept. 7, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The firm that had barely survived:</span> Note
that Lehman’s fiscal year ran from December 1 through November 30.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I don’t want you to tell me why we
can’t”:</span> McDonald’s account of Gelband’s unsuccessful efforts to
get Lehman to pull back on its real-estate exposure is corroborated by
reports in <span class="italic">New York</span> magazine and the
<span class="italic">Observer</span> (London). <span class="italic">New
York</span> reported that Gelband had pointedly told Fuld, “The world is
changing. We have to rethink our business model.” Fuld retorted that
Gelband was too conservative. Steve Fishman, “Burning Down His House,”
<span class="italic">New York</span>, Dec. 8, 2008. The
<span class="italic">Observer</span> quoted “Lehman insiders” who said
Gelband railed against Lehman’s investment in subprime lenders as well
as the huge stake that
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>Lehman bought in the United States’s largest
apartment company. Nick Mathiason, Heather Connon, and Richard Wachman,
“Risky Business: Banking’s Big Question, Why Didn’t Anyone Stop Them?”
<span class="italic">Observer</span>, Feb. 15, 2009. I tried to arrange
an interview with Fuld through his attorney, Patricia Hynes. In an
e-mail reply in 2009, she told me, “Mr. Fuld is not doing any
interviews.”

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It was quite hard to stand in the way”:</span>
Former Lehman executive Andrew Gowers was quoted in Mathiason, Connon,
and Wachman, “Risky Business.” Another former top Lehman executive told
the <span class="italic">New York Times</span> that it was unrealistic
to have expected Lehman and other Wall Street firms to exercise
self-restraint: “From a policy perspective, the regulators have to step
in. It would be an awful lot to ask the Street to not look for revenue
opportunities where their competitors are finding revenue.” Louise Story
and Landon Thomas Jr., “Tales from Lehman’s Crypt,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Sept. 12, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the SOBs knew how to get to me”:</span> E-mail
interview with Irv Ackelsberg.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Arnall’s nomination process:</span> Transcript,
“Hearing of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee,” Federal News
service, Oct. 20, 2005. See also coverage by the Associated Press,
<span class="italic">Washington Post</span>, <span class="italic">Los
Angeles Times</span>, <span class="italic">Roll Call</span>, and other
news outlets.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA334.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>By the time the committee held its first
hearing:</span> Despite his conversion into one of the GOP’s key money
men, Arnall also enjoyed support from Democrats he had cultivated over
the years. These included New Mexico governor Bill Richardson, a
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page349"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>2008 presidential hopeful. Richardson wrote that
he could “attest to the strength of \[Arnall’s\] personal convictions,
his commitment to community and his deep love for our country.” A
spokesman said Richardson considered Arnall a friend and that Richardson
“respects him for being a leader of a very large company.” Tory Newmyer,
“Arnall Secures Outside Help,” <span class="italic">Roll Call</span>,
Dec. 5, 2005; and Steve Terrell, “Roundhouse Roundup: Governor’s
Ameriquest Contacts in Question,” <span class="italic">Santa Fe New
Mexican</span>, May 18, 2006.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>the vote was deadlocked:</span> Connecticut
senator Chris Dodd reluctantly joined his fellow Democrats in voting
against Arnall. He considered Arnall a friend. “He did a fundraiser for
me,” Dodd explained. “I don’t like voting against the man.” Tory
Newmyer, “Floor Fight Looms over Arnall Vote,” <span class="italic">Roll
Call,</span> Nov. 9, 2005.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We take great pride”:</span> One critic of the
nomination, consumer attorney Ira Rheingold, went on ABC’s
<span class="italic">Nightline</span> and denounced the Senate’s vote as
an insult to the borrowers who’d been defrauded by Arnall’s company.
“The notion that the person who owns that company would become a U.S.
representative to a foreign country, really, is absolutely appalling to
anybody who’s watched Ameriquest’s practices over the years.” Rheinhold
suspected he understood, though, why Arnall might want to seek the job:
“I think he’s got all the money in the world he could possibly want. And
I think what he’s looking
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>for…is legitimacy. He’s looking for recognition.
And I think it’s sort of the icing. You know, money can buy you an awful
lot. And, you know…being called Mr. Ambassador is a pretty cool thing, I
guess. And when you own everything else, why not?”\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span> A <span class="italic">Nightline</span>
correspondent also talked to Wade Henderson, the director of the
Leadership Conference on Civil Rights and one of Arnall’s biggest
supporters. “Have you ever seen any of Ameriquest’s paperwork?” she
asked. “’Cause I have some here to show you if you haven’t.”\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span> “I’ve seen some of it,” Henderson answered.
“I’m disappointed, I’m profoundly disappointed, that some of these
practices that have now come to light would be associated with
Ameriquest. Because the company that I know, the company that I had
thought achieved a pretty substantial status, as a company engaged in
fair practices, had somehow slipped and fallen and run afoul of existing
practices. And I think that’s terrible. And, yes, I do believe it should
be addressed. But at the end of the day, I’ll stand by the fact that I
think Roland Arnall is a man of integrity.” ABC News, “Dutch
Trea<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>t? Just Dessert?”
<span class="italic">Nightline</span>, Jan. 24, 2006.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>In Massachusetts, Deval Patrick was
fighting:</span> Coverage in the <span class="italic">Boston
Globe</span> and <span class="italic">Boston Herald</span>, especially
Frank Phillips, “Patrick Tied to Company Under Fire,”
<span class="italic">Boston Globe</span>, Apr. 20, 2005; and Dave Wedge
and Kimberly Atkins, “Deval Denies Lobbying Obama for Envoy,”
<span class="italic">Boston Herald</span>, Oct. 21, 2006.

<span class="bold1"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>15. Collapse</span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>George and Evelyn Lee:</span> Interviews with
Evelyn Lee and with her attorney, Sharon Withers, as well as the Lees’
loan documents and filings in <span class="italic">Lee v. Wolverine
Builder LLC et al.</span>, Tenth Circuit Court of Michigan, 2007. The
case was settled on undisclosed terms.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA335.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>the subject of twenty-five complaints:</span>
Michigan regulators dismissed some of the
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page350"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>complaints, but as of mid-2007 the state had
upheld eight of them and referred others for investigation. Real
Financial’s attorney said the allegations stemmed from an unfavorable
economy that had sparked rising foreclosures as well as unjustified
complaints against lenders and brokers. Lehman said it only checked to
see whether brokers were licensed in their states, not whether the
licensing agencies had received complaints about them. Lehman said it
removed Real Financial from its broker list after Evelyn Lee filed her
lawsuit. See Michael Hudson, “Lending a Hand: How Wall Street Stoked
the<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> Mortgage Meltdown; Lehman and Others
Transformed the Market for Riskiest Borrowers,”
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.0.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>,
June 27, 2007.

<span class="italic">“stormed out of a meeting”: Operative Plasterers
and Cement Masons International Association Local 262 Annuity Fund v.
Richard S. Fuld et al.</span>, U.S. District Court for the Southern
District of New York, 2008, pp. 57–58 and 72–73.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>First Magnus:</span> Local coverage, including
Christie Smythe, “Gov’t Report Slams 1st Magnus,”
<span class="italic">Arizona Daily Star</span>, Aug. 9, 2008; Gabriela
Rico and Josh Brodesky, “First Magnus Executives Are Sued for \$1
Billion,” <span class="italic">Arizona Daily Star</span>, Feb. 27, 2009;
Josh Brodesky, “Suit Says First Magnus Officers Fueled Crisis,”
<span class="italic">Arizona Daily Star</span>, Feb. 28, 2009; and Joe
Pangburn, “\$1 Billion Lawsuit: First Magnus Wasn’t a Victim: It Caused
Credit Crisis,” <span class="italic">Inside Tucson Business</span>, Mar.
6, 2009. See also <span class="italic">Romero v. First Magnus</span>,
U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“I’m standing in the middle of a
cornfield”:</span> Interviews with Steven Jernigan, who worked as a
senior fraud analyst at Argent from May 2005 to December 2006.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>a con man named Robert Andrew Penn:</span> See
James R. Hagerty and Michael Hudson, “Town’s Residents Say They Were
Targets of Big Mortgage Fraud,” <span class="italic">Wall Street
Journal</span>, Sept. 28, 2006; and Erika D. Smith, Madhusmita Bora, and
J. K. Wall, “Red Flags Preceded Home-Fraud Lawsuit,”
<span class="italic">Indianapolis Star</span>, Oct. 1, 2006. Penn
pleaded guilty to three felonies and was sentenced to seven years in
prison. Details of his scheme are described in an October 7, 2009,
document, “Stipulated Factual Basis,” signed by Penn, his attorney, and
the prosecutor. See <span class="italic">USA v. Penn</span>, U.S.
District Court for the Southern
Dis<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>trict of Indiana, 2009, Case No.
1:09-CR-114-01-DFH-KPF.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“You’ve got to stop”:</span> In a written
response, an ACC Capital spokesman did not specifically respond to my
questions about whether Steve Jernigan had been instructed to back off
on investigating higher-ups within Argent who turned a “blind eye” to
fraud. The spokesman said: “The company terminated Steve Jernigan for
cause, and we also do not believe he is a credible source for your
book.” As for the Robert Penn case, the spokesman said that “Argent
aggressively pursued its criminal and civil options against the
individuals and corporations who perpetrated this fraud…. Argent
repurchased ever<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.5.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>y loan that was identified as problematic—more
than two hundred loans in all.” In the wake of the Penn case, the
spokesman said, Argent significantly increased its fraud detection
efforts.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA336.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“It’s just like somebody flipped a
switch”:</span> James R. Hagerty and Michael Corkery, “After the Boom:
Housing Slump Proves Painful for Some Owners and Builders,”
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, Aug. 23, 2006.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page351" class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“a call by a rich man”:</span> David A. Mittell,
“Anatomy of a Telephone Call, from One Rich Guy to Another,”
<span class="italic">Patriot Ledger</span>, Mar. 17, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“the alter ego”:</span> Borrowers’ First Amended
Consolidated Class Action Complaint, filed June 18, 2007, in
<span class="italic">In Re: Ameriquest Mortgage Co. Mortgage Lending
Practices Litigation</span>, U.S. District Court for the Northern
District of Illinois, MDL No. 1715, Lead Case No. 05-cv-07097.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Wayne Lee: Lee v. Ameriquest</span>, Orange
County Superior Court, 2007, as well as Lee’s May 9, 2007, deposition in
<span class="italic">In Re: Ameriquest Mortgage Co. Mortgage Practices
Litigation</span>.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“We all saw the mortgage stars”:</span> Andrew
Galvin, “Is There a Backlash Against Former Mortgage Workers?”
<span class="italic">Orange County Register</span>, Feb. 12, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Other communities in California:</span> “Priest
Aims to Save Flock from Foreclosure,” Associated Press, Aug. 5, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Ameriquest and Argent accounted for:</span>
Based on data compiled by the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the
Currency; letter from John C. Dugan, Comptroller of the Currency, to
Elizabeth Warren, chair, Congressional Oversight Panel, Feb. 12, 2009.\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span> In the letter, the OCC reported that as of
early 2009 the ten worst foreclosure zones in the United States were (1)
Detroit (with 22.9 percent of subprime and Alt-A loans made between 2005
and 2007 in foreclosure); (2) Cleveland (21.6 percent); (3) Stockton,
California (21.5 percent); (4) Sacramento (18 percent); (5)
Riverside–San Bernardino, California (16.1 percent); (6) Memphis (15.6
percent); (7) Miami–Fort Lauderdale (14.3 percent); (8) Bakersfield,
California (14.3 percent); (9) Denver (14 percent); and (10) Las Vegas
(13.9 percent).\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span> In those ten zones, the following ten lenders
had the highest foreclosure totals for loans made between 2005 and 2007:
(1) Ameriquest/Argent (with 14,854 subprime and Alt-A loan
foreclosures); (2) New Century (14,120); (3) Long Beach (11,736); (4)
WMC (10,283); (5) Fremont (8,635); (6) Option One (8,334); (7) First
Franklin (8,037); (8) Countrywide (4,736); (9) Resmae (3,558); and (10)
American Home (2,954). In looking at the lenders with the most
foreclosures in the ten zones, the OCC ranked Argent and Ameriquest
separately, which would plant Argent third on its list (with
10,728<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.7.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> foreclosures) and Ameriquest ninth (with
4,126). But because these companies were owned by the same man and run
under the same corporate flag, ACC Capital, I recalculated the rankings
by combining Argent’s and Ameriquest’s numbers. Of the top six companies
on the list, the only one not based in Orange County was WMC Mortgage,
which was headquartered just down the highway in San Diego. No. 9,
Resmae, also an Orange County company, was founded by former executives
who had worked under Roland Arnall at Long Beach Mortgage. Other Orange
County lenders that landed farther down the list included No. 16,
People’s <span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.7.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>Choice (with 1,783 foreclosures), and No. 17,
BNC (1,769), Lehman’s subprime mortgage lending unit.\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA337.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span> These figures are a snapshot of the toll of
subprime lending, but they don’t show the full force of its devastation;
they don’t include foreclosures on loans made in the earlier boom years
(2002–2004) and they don’t reflect foreclosures that have
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page352"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>been filed since early 2009 on any 2005–2007
loans. Using data only for loans made from 2005 to 2007, in particular,
understates the foreclosure rates among Ameriquest borrowers since the
lender drastically reduced its loan volume in 2006 and 2007 as a result
of the limitations put on it by its settlement with state authorities.

<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

<span class="italic">Implode-O-Meter:</span> By the start of 2010, the
number of imploded lenders listed on the site had reached 374. See
<span class="xrefURL"><a href="http://ml-implode.com/"
class="calibre6">http://ml-implode.com/</a></span>.

<span class="italic">Mozilo’s home-loan giant had been done in:</span>
Defending the company’s practices, a Countrywide spokesman, Rick Simon,
said, “No one…could have foreseen the unprecedented combination of
events that led to the problems borrowers, lenders and investors face
with many of these loans today.” Gretchen Morgenson and Geraldine
Fabrikant, “Countrywide’s Chief Salesman and Defender,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Nov. 11, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Countrywide did little to pull back:</span> See
especially Paul Muolo and Mathew Padilla, <span class="italic">Chain of
Blame: How Wall Street Caused the Mortgage and Credit Crisis</span>
(Hoboken, N.J.: John Wiley & Sons, 2008), p. 303; E. Scott Reckard, “Is
Angelo Mozilo a Villain or Just Vilified?” <span class="italic">Los
Angeles Times</span>, Aug. 30, 2009; and E. Scott Reckard and Jim
Puzzanghera, “Countrywide’s Angelo Mozilo Is Target of Federal Lawsuit,”
<span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, June 5, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Lehman wasn’t as secure as it claimed:</span>
This account of Lehman’s failure and the global meltdown is based on
coverage by Bloomberg News, the <span class="italic">Guardian</span>
(London), the <span class="italic">Times</span> (London), the
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, and the
<span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, and in particular
Carrick Mollenkamp, Susanne Craig, Jeffrey McCracken, and Jon

Capital Belied the Firm’s Public Optimism,” <span class="italic">Wall
Street Journal</span>, Oct. 6, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“There is no way a person like me”:</span> Mark
Pittman and Bob Ivry, “London Suicide Connects Lehman Lesson Missed by
Hong Kong Woman,” Bloomberg News, Sept. 10, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.5.0"

volume”:</span> Pierre Thomas and Lauren Pearle, “WaMu Insiders Claim

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>The mortgage meltdown was a ticklish
subject:</span> John R. Emshwiller, “A Top Obama Fund-Raiser Had Ties to
Failed Bank,” <span class="italic">Wall Street Journal</span>, July 21,

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Community Reinvestment Act, Fannie Mae, and
Freddie Mac:</span> Ronald Campbell, “Most Subprime Lenders Weren’t
Subject to Federal Lending Law,” <span class="italic">Orange County
Register</span>, Nov. 16, 2008; and Zachary A. Goldfarb, “Fannie,
Freddie Become Hot Topic in Campaign,” <span class="italic">Washington
Post</span>, Oct. 9, 2008.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA338.w.1.8.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“You’re becoming irrelevant”:</span> Charles
Duhigg, “Pressured to Take More Risks, Fannie Reached Tipping Point,”
<span class="italic">New York Times</span>, Oct. 4, 2008. In late 2008,
in the wake of Lehman Brothers’ bankruptcy, Republicans on the U.S.
House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform issued a report that
managed to get Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac’s role exactly backward.
“Lehman Brothers didn’t cause this mess but it certainly jumped head
first into trying to make money on securitizing mortgage-backed
instruments. They followed on the heels of Fannie Mae and
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_page353"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Freddie Mac and for precisely the same reasons.
If we understand the initial cause of the cancer at Fannie and Freddie,
then we can understand how it metastasized to Lehman Brothers, Wachovia,
Countrywide and beyond.” Lehman had been a leader in the market for
subprime loans long before Fannie and Freddie followed Wall Street into
subprime. From 1996 to 2006, in every year except 2001, Lehman ranked
first or second on the list of top underwriters of subprime
mortgage–backed securities, according to <span class="italic">Inside
Mortgage Finance</span>.\
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span> As CNBC correspondent David Faber has written:
“Wall Street rushed into the vacuum created by the
<span class="italic">absence</span> of Fannie and Freddie in 2003–2005.”
Under pressure from Congress and federal regulators in the wake of
accounting scandals, “Fannie and Freddie retreated from the market they
had dominated for the past twenty years. They began to buy fewer
mortgages in a period where people were buying and refinancing more
homes than ever before.” As a result, Fannie and Freddie’s share of the
secondary mortgage market dropped from 70 percent in 2003 to just 30
percent in 2006. See David Faber,
<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.1.1.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>And Then the Roof Caved In</span> (Hoboken,
N.J.: John Wiley & Sons, 2009), pp. 63–66.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Mark Glover: Glover v. Citibank et al</span>.,
Los Angeles Superior Court, 2007. Glover could not say how much he
reaped from the settlement of his lawsuit against Ameriquest, but court
papers noted that he had won “a sizable settlement from a legal suit.”
His case against Citibank was later transferred out of court to
arbitration.

Mail</span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> (Toronto), Feb. 13, 2009.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA339.w.1.4.0"

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA340.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>he experienced a transformation:</span> Travis
Paules wasn’t the only former Ameriquest salesman who made a change in
his life. Mark Bomchill had turned whistle-blower in our February 2005
exposé in the <span class="italic">Los Angeles Times</span>, condemning
the company’s boiler-room tactics and recalling the manager who stalked
between the loan officers’ cubicles like “a little Hitler.” After the
story ran, he provided testimony in court cases and continued to speak
to the media about the company’s practices. “I feel bad that I was part
of this. I feel like I was one of the Enron people who ripped off the
little guy,”<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA340.w.1.4.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> Bomchill told National Public Radio. “A lot of
Ameriquest customers were not educated. They were vulnerable to this
kind of deception. They were trusting. And because of that, they lost a
lot.” See Chris Arnold, “Former Ameriquest Workers Tell of Deception,”
<span class="italic">Morning Edition</span>, National Public Radio, May
14, 2007.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA340.w.1.5.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Bank of America case: Pope v. Bank of
America</span>, U.S. District Court for the Southern District of
Mississippi, 2004. The lawsuit called EquiCredit, Bank of America’s
former subprime lending subsidiary, “a notorious lender” that had used
“a network of corrupt contractors, real estate brokers, mortgage loan
brokers, appraisers and settlement agents” to fund home loans “that were
shockingly unfair and abusive.” The lawsuit alleged that Clara Pope, a
sixty-seven-year-old widow who suffered from diabetes and other serious
health problems, had been stuck with an EquiCredit mortgage she’d had
n<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA340.w.1.5.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>o hope of repaying. The suit also raised the
question of whether her signature had been forged on the paperwork. The
case was settled in late 2004 on undisclosed terms. Don Barrett, another
one of the Mississippi litigators on the Lehman case, served as
Canavan’s cocounsel in the case.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA340.w.1.6.0"
class="calibre2"></span>“built like a house of cards”: In Re: First
Alliance Mortgage Co.</span>, 471 F.3d 977 (9th Cir. 2006).

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA340.w.1.7.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Prentiss Cox:</span> Prentiss Cox, “The Proposed
Consumer Financial Protection Agency: Implications for Consumers and the
FTC,” testimony before the U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce,
July 8, 2009. The main problem, Cox said during his testimony, was that
the nation’s regulatory system was “thoroughly dominated” by the
thinking and needs of lenders and their allies rather than the needs of
average consumers and homeowners.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA341"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA341.w.0.0.0"

Interview with Brian Chisick.

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA341.w.1.1.0"

<span class="italic"><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA341.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Carolyn Pittman:</span> Interviews with Carolyn
Pittman and her attorney, Lynn Drysdale of Jacksonville Area Legal Aid;
Caren Burmeister, “Beaches Woman Caught in a Foreclosure Cycle,”
<span class="italic">Florida Times-Union</span>, Sept. 22, 2007; and
“Defendants Motion to Strike Count I, Answer, Amended Affirmative
Defenses, Amended Counterclaims and Demand for Jury Trial,”
<span class="italic">Deutsche Bank v. Pittman</span>, Duval County
(Fla.) Circuit Court, 2007. Unlike many beleaguered homeowners, Pittman
was fortunate to find attorneys to help her fight to save her home.
Jacksonville Area Legal Aid, a not-for-profit legal clinic that has
gained a<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA341.w.1.2.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span> national reputation as an
anti-foreclosur<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA342"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA342.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>e campaigner, took up her cause and stuck with
her for years. A report from New York University Law School’s Brennan
Center for Justice found that many homeowners were losing their homes
because they lacked legal representation. Nonprofit legal aid clinics
had been “besieged with requests for foreclosure assistance.” In
Connecticut, more than 60 percent of homeowners facing foreclosure in
2007–2008 did not have counsel. In Staten Island, New York, 91 percent
of foreclosures on subprime or “non-traditional” mortgages “proceeded
without full legal representation” for the homeowners. See Melanca Clark
wit<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA342.w.0.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>h Maggie Barron, “Foreclosures: A Crisis in
Legal Representation,” Brennan Center for Justice, Nov. 6, 2009; and
Alex Ulam, “Stacked Deck Against Homeowners,”
<span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA342.w.0.0.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_not01.html_GBS.PA342.w.0.0.0.3"
class="calibre2"></span><span class="italic">The Nation</span>, Dec. 22,
2009.

<div class="calibre3">

## <span class="bold">Author’s Note and Acknowledgments</span>

</div>

<div class="calibre3">

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA343.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>This is a book of investigative reporting. I
brought no special skills in financial analysis to this project. What I
brought mainly was a willingness to read reports and court documents and
pick up the phone and ask people to talk to me about things that, for
many, were painful or incriminating. I read hundreds of lawsuits, read
thousands of pages of court transcripts, and interviewed hundreds of
people over the past five years. Virtually all of the key sources for
this book spoke to me on the record. Their names are indicated in the
text or in the source notes. The accounts of
som<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA343.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>e come from court transcripts or other official
documents. A few spoke to me on a not-for-attribution basis. I’ve tried
to identify them by indicating where they worked and what kind of job
they were doing during the time they described.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA343.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>I was heartened by the number of former industry
insiders who felt compelled to tell what they knew about the bad
practices in the mortgage business. A few merit special notice. They
include Mark Glover, Stephen Kuhn, Travis Paules, and Greg Walling. They
were willing to talk frankly about their years in the industry and about
things they’d done that they regretted, in large part because they
wanted to set things right.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA343.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Other folks who provided substantial help in my
reporting include Terry Rouch, Angie Moreschi, Melissa Huelsman, Bill
Brennan, Howard Rothbloom, Mark Adelson, John Dewey, Kathleen Engel,
Gregory Burke, Patricia McCoy, Kevin Stein, Larry Gabriel, Dan
Immergluck, <span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_page358"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Lynn Drysdale, David Humphreys, Sheila Canavan,
Josh Zinner, Jude Lopez, Chris Peterson, Dennis Rivelli, Ira Rheingold,
Prentiss Cox, Tom James, Chuck Cross, and Chris Carpenter. One person
who deserves special thanks is Bob Labrador, the former treasurer at
Long Beach Savings and Loan. When I first called Bob, he was skeptical.
He asked lots of questions about who I was and what I was doing. After
he was satisfied I had done my homework, he became a supporter of my
work. He put me in touch with former colleagues and drove me around
Orange County, giving me a tour of the landscape
<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>of the county’s subprime lending industry. His
help was crucial to my understanding of Roland Arnall’s early years as a
developer and lender. Another former Long Beach executive who was a big
help was Mark Schuerman. He, too, talked to me for hours, answering
question after question without complaint. I should add, though, that
neither Bob nor Mark necessarily agrees with all of the conclusions that
I reach in this book and shouldn’t be held responsible for what I’ve
written. The same holds for all the other people who helped me piece
together this story.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.0.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

I drew on many publications in weaving together this narrative. Two
deserve special mention: <span class="italic">Mortgage Lender
Implode-O-Meter</span> and <span class="italic">Inside Mortgage
Finance</span>. <span class="italic">IMF</span> is a rich and definitive
source of data on the mortgage industry. Unless otherwise noted,
mortgage volume data quoted in this book for the subprime industry or
specific lenders come from <span class="italic">IMF</span>’s reports.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span><img src="OEBPS/Images/sp.jpg" class="epubimage" alt="image" /><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.3.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>

I’ve spent the better part of two decades investigating predatory
lending. I began reporting on the subject in 1992, thanks to a
fellowship from the Alicia Patterson Foundation, an organization that
supports in-depth journalism. APF’s director, Margaret Engel, provided
advice and encouragement. Katherine Boo, then an editor at
<span class="italic">Washington Monthly</span>, helped me develop my
first piece on lending abuses, “Stealing Home,” which appeared in the
magazine’s June 1992 issue. <span class="italic">Southern
Exposure</span> was a home for my reporting on the subject over a period
of ten years; Eric Bates, Bob Hall, and Chris
K<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA344.w.1.3.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>romm and others at
<span class="italic">SE</span> were willing to edit and publish long
cover packages about <span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_page359"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>businesses that market to disadvantaged
consumers. I was project editor and coauthor of a package of stories in
the magazine’s Summer 2003 issue titled, “Poverty, Inc.” A decade later,
I called Gary Ashwill, the magazine’s managing editor, and pitched him a
story about Citigroup’s role in the subprime market. I’d struck out with
other publications, because they weren’t interested in the story or
because they didn’t want to invest the space to tell the story with the
depth that I believe the story required. Gary said they would take it as
a cover story. When I asked, “How
muc<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>h space can we have?,” he gave an answer that is
rarely heard in modern American journalism: “How much space do we need?”
The magazine devoted forty-eight pages in its Fall 2003 issue to
“Banking on Misery,” a package of articles about Citigroup and other
businesses that target poor and minority consumers.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>Greg Bates of Common Courage Press encouraged me
to put together my first book on the subject,
<span class="italic">Merchants of Misery: How Corporate America Profits
from Poverty</span> (Monroe, Me.: Common Courage Press, 1996). The book
was a collection of my writings as well as pieces by Penny Loeb, Eric
Rorer, Bill Minutaglio, Rita Jensen, Alix Freedman, Kim Nauer, Martha
Brannigan, Adam Feuerstein, and others.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>At the <span class="italic">Los Angeles
Times</span>, I had the pleasure of working with a group of top-notch
editors. Deborah Nelson and Rick Wartzman saw the potential in my
reporting on Ameriquest, and John Corrigan oversaw the investigation and
edited the stories with tough love. <span class="italic">Times</span>
staff writer Scott Reckard was a great reporting partner. He’s a
tireless worker, a fine reporter, and an all-round good guy. Many
passages in this book are built on the reporting that Scott and I did
together.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>At the <span class="italic">Wall Street
Journal</span>, where I worked in 2006 and 2007, a number of colleagues
supported my efforts to report on abuses in the subprime market,
including Sue Craig, Susan Pulliam, Mike Siconolfi, Bob Hagerty, Alix
Freedman, and Nik Deogan. Others at the
<span class="italic">Journal</span> provided support as I tried to learn
the ins and outs of Wall Street, including Serena Ng, Greg Zuckerman,
Karen Richardson, Shefali Anand, Kate Kelly, Jesse Drucker, and Joanna
Slater.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA345.w.1.4.0"
class="calibre2"></span>This book was independent of my work at the
Center for Responsible Lending, where I earned my paycheck as a
researcher from late 2007 through the spring of 2010. Nothing in it
should be automatically <span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_page360"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.0.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.0.0"
class="calibre2"></span>deemed to reflect the views and policies of CRL,
and it was not vetted or approved by anyone in a position of authority
at the center. That said, my work with the smart and dedicated people at
CRL greatly benefited my understanding of how mortgage markets work and
of the problems of average consumers. CRL is a nonprofit policy and
research outfit headquartered in Durham, North Carolina. I went to work
for CRL because I needed a job and because CRL was an organization that
had gotten it right. While industry groups touted the benefits of
subprime and news organizations for the most
<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.0.0.1"
class="calibre2"></span>part downplayed the problems in the industry,
CRL was doing well-documented research that exposed the dicey practices
in the subprime business and accurately predicted a coming wave of
foreclosures. Once I got to CRL, Jim  Overton and I worked together on
research projects focusing on  Countrywide Financial, IndyMac Bank, and
the Office of Thrift Supervision. Jim proved to be a dogged, kind, and
perceptive collaborator. Eric Stein, a superb editor, thoughtful
colleague, and first-rate boss, oversaw much of my work. Many others
provided encouragement and enlightenment: Martin Eakes, Keith
Corbet<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.0.0.2"
class="calibre2"></span>t, Mary Moore, Kathleen Day, Mike Calhoun,
Aracely Panameño, Keith Ernst, Wei Li, Sam Rogers, Ellen Schloemer, Eric
Halperin, Caryn Becker, Lisa Pittman, Daniel Mosteller, Sharon Reuss,
Sara Weed, Evan Fuguet, Paul Leonard, Chris Kukla, Ellen Harnick, Nina
Simon, Romy Parzik, Toni van Rijssen, and many more.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.0.0.3"
class="calibre2"></span><span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.1.0"
class="calibre2"></span>

I also want to thank the folks at the Center for Public Integrity, where
I now work as a staff writer. They include Bill Buzenberg, Gordon
Witkin, Julie Vorman, Brian Grow, and many others. The Center is one of
the oldest and most respected of the nonprofit journalism operations,
and I’m honored to be part of that tradition.

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.2.0"
class="calibre2"></span>I also want to thank friends and colleagues who
have supported me. They include Barry Yeoman, Mary Kane, Jeff Bailey,

Mencimer, Ron Nixon, Jim Campen, Christine Richard, Roland Lazenby, Jim

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA346.w.1.3.0"
class="calibre2"></span>I especially want to express gratitude to the
folks who read all or parts of my manuscript and offered insightful

<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA347.w.1.1.0"

Many thanks should go to my agent, Sam Stoloff, who believed in this

acros<span id="9780805090468_ack01.html_GBS.PA348"

Finally, I want to send thanks and love to my family, which supported
